item.content:encoded:
Game 4 of the World Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays begins at 8:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, October 27, televised by FOX. The Brewers are favored with a 1.75x payout to win on PrizePicks.
The Milwaukee Brewers lead 3-0 in the World Series after routing the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 in Game 3 on Monday. Milwaukee is now one win away from securing the franchise's first World Series championship, while Tampa Bay faces elimination and must win four consecutive games to complete an improbable comeback.
The Rays will turn to SP Griffin Jax in Game 4, hoping the right-hander can slow down a Brewers lineup that has dominated the World Series. Milwaukee has not announced its starting pitcher, potentially setting up another bullpen game as the club looks to complete the sweep.
Below, we'll break down our Brewers vs. Rays prediction and picks for Tuesday's World Series Game 4, including the winner and player picks for PrizePicks.
{{mlb_offer_banner="/style-system/ui-components-playbook"}}
Brewers vs. Rays Prediction, Winner Payout, Over/Under for World Series Game 4
Milwaukee enters Game 4 as the road favorite, returning a 1.75x payout if it wins outright.
Here are the full payouts for the Brewers vs. Rays game. PrizePicks data is live at the time of writing and is subject to change.
Make your Brewers vs. Rays prediction on the winner on PrizePicks.
Unless otherwise noted, data used in this article is from FanGraphs, Baseball Savant, and MLB.com.
Griffin Jax (3.41 xFIP) will take the ball for Tampa Bay as the Rays' season hangs in the balance. The right-hander finished the regular season 8-10 with a 3.53 ERA and 116 strikeouts.
He faces a tough assignment against a Milwaukee offense that has consistently put runners on base throughout the World Series, but his regular-season home success could help him tonight.
Jax has struggled during the postseason, allowing 4 earned runs over six innings in his previous playoff appearances.
We can talk all we want about Tampa’s pitching plans, but ultimately the Rays offense will need a much better showing against Milwaukee's pitching staff if they want to save their season.
Despite being so good at getting runners on base and capitalizing with runners in scoring position during the regular season, the Rays managed just 1 run and struggled to generate sustained offense in Game 3. Those same issues plagued Tampa Bay in the first two games of this series.
The Brewers' pitching plans remain uncertain heading into tonight. Milwaukee has not announced a starter, and a bullpen-heavy approach seems most likely with the championship within reach.
The Brewers used LHP Robert Gasser in Game 3, and he delivered one of the postseason's most dominant starts, allowing just 1 hit over six innings while striking out 6.
Gasser's performance gave Milwaukee's bullpen valuable rest, which could prove significant if the Brewers need multiple relievers to get through Game 4. Milwaukee's pitching staff has been outstanding throughout the postseason, allowing just 7 runs across its first three World Series games.
The Brewers offense has stolen the show this World Series. At one point last night, they recorded eight straight two-out hits to blow the game wide open — a truly magnificent team feat on the grandest stage of all.

Brewers vs. Rays Prediction on Winner for World Series Game 4 – 10/27/26
Here are the key stats and trends behind our Brewers vs. Rays prediction on the winner for Tuesday's World Series Game 4.
- It feels insane to fade this Brewers team right now, but I can’t see Tampa Bay getting swept at home, especially considering how dominant its been at Tropicana Field all season.
- The Rays went 58-27-0 at home this season; their 68.2% home win rate ranked second in baseball, behind the Brewers.
- Griffin Jax's regular-season home xFIP was 2.82, a full run better than his 4.08 road xFIP.
- The Brewers didn’t need to use any of their high-leverage arms last night, and neither did the Rays, who essentially conceded the game in the fifth inning. This leaves Tampa Bay’s best relievers ready to come in, and perhaps used slightly more aggressively than Milwaukee’s, given the lack of margin for error in an elimination game.
- While the Brewers’ pen has been awesome this postseason, their 3.57 xFIP sits well above a 1.34 ERA. Also, their .220 BABIP could signal regression in what is shaping up to be a bullpen game for the Brew Crew.
- The Rays offense has been better at home, owning a 108 wRC+ at the Trop compared to a 100 wRC+ on the road during the regular season.
Brewers vs. Rays Picks, Player Stats for World Series on PrizePicks – 10/27/26
Here are two Brewers vs. Rays player picks to consider on PrizePicks for Tuesday's World Series Game 4. Today's MLB picks include Jackson Chourio and Griffin Jax.

- This guy is simply unfadeable right now. He's recorded three straight multi-hit games to start the World Series and cleared this projection in all three as well.
- He has also cleared this projection in eight of the Brewers' 11 postseason games (72.7%).
- After recording no steals in any game before the World Series, Chourio has shown more willingness to run, already swiping 3 bags in this series, giving him yet another way to clear this projection.

- He has specifically dominated LHB, striking them out to the tune of a 12.92 K/9 to go along with a 2.12 xFIP at home this season. The Brewers lineup projects to have six left-handed hitters tonight.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are favored to take Game 3 on Monday, but their chances of capturing their first ever World Series title have dwindled.
The Rays jumped out to a 4-0 first inning lead in Game 2, but through the game’s final eight innings the offense sputtered and the defense, nor pitching from ace Drew Rasmussen, was as sharp as needed to hold down the Brewers, who earned a 5-4 victory.
The pair of one-run victories in Milwaukee have put the Brewers in prime position for their first title. Nearly 81% of MLB teams that have generated a 2-0 series lead in the World Series have gone on to win the title.
To disrupt that statistic, the Rays will need to find a way to win Game 3. Kalshi traders make their odds 53% as of Monday morning.
For informational purposes only. Not trading advice. See full disclaimer below. Kalshi is the Official Prediction Market Partner of the Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Dodgers, San Francisco Giants, San Diego Padres, and Boston Red Sox.
World Series Game 3 Odds: Rays favored in home ballpark
Right-handed pitcher Freddy Peralta had a rough start to his 2026 campaign when pitching for the New York Mets. But after being dealt to the Rays, he’s unlocked a former version of himself, one the Milwaukee Brewers know quite well. Peralta pitched for the Brewers for eight seasons before being traded to the Mets in the offseason. The Mets dealt him to the Rays at the trade deadline.
As such, now he’ll need to square off against his former team in World Series Game 3, looking to extend an incredible stretch of pitching which saw him earn ALCS MVP honors.
Across three starts and one relief appearance this postseason, Peralta has thrown 16.2 innings and allowed just two earned runs, good for a 1.08 ERA.
But the Brewers represent a level up offensively. Milwaukee finished the regular season tied for first in wRC+ against right-handed starters and led the league in on-base percentage and batting average against the handedness.
On the other hand, the Rays will draw left-handed starter Robert Gasser. Like the rest of the Milwaukee staff, Gasser has been fantastic this postseason, throwing nine innings over the course of two starts and allowing just one earned run.
Southpaws have been a challenge for the Rays this season, with the team ranking 26th against lefties in terms of wRC+ during the regular season. Even if they are able to get through Gasser, the Milwaukee bullpen features lefties JoJo Romero, DL Hall, and Aaron Ashby, and has been nearly unhittable, collectively posting a 1.23 ERA in nearly 51 innings this postseason.
Nevertheless, Kalshi traders make the Rays, who posted a 55-26 record at home during the regular season, slight favorites at 53% in Game 3.
The Rays overcame a 2-1 deficit in the ALCS, but they face a stiffer test against baseball’s top team in the World Series.
Regardless of the Game 3 winner, Game 4 will take place on Tuesday in Tampa Bay. In early trading, Kalshi traders make the Brewers slight favorites on the road in that game, pricing them at 50%.
Should a Game 5 be necessary, it will take place on Wednesday in Tampa Bay. If Games 6 or 7 are required, those will take place back in Milwaukee after a travel day.
Through two games, Brewers catcher William Contreras is the favorite for World Series MVP, according to Kalshi traders.
Contreras is trading around 38% to earn the award while outfielder Jackson Chourio is trading at 17% and left-handed reliever Aaron Ashby is priced at 15%.
In their two home victories, Contreras has notched four hits in eight at-bats and driven in two runs for Milwaukee. Plus, he’s thrown out multiple runners attempting to steal and helped manage a pitching staff through two tense one-run victories.
Chourio has posted similar stats, netting four hits in his nine at-bats, while stealing two bases and cutting down a runner at the plate with an outfield assist during Game 2.
Though less heralded coming into the series, Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby has been dominant all postseason, pitching 15.2 innings without allowing a single run. That includes more than three innings of World Series play in which he’s only allowed one hit.
Down 2-0, the highest priced Ray player is Junior Caminero, who is trading around 6% to win the award.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Francisco Lindor Wins 2026 Roberto Clemente Award, Continuing a Proud Puerto Rican Legacy
item.dc:creator: Eddie Lennon; Staff Writer
item.description: Francisco Lindor has accomplished just about everything a baseball player could hope to achieve. He's a five-time All-Star, a four-time Silver Slugger and one of the most recognizable shortstops in Major League Baseball. But on October 26, Lindor received an honor that has little to do with his numbers at the plate or his performance on the field. item.content:encoded:
Francisco Lindor has accomplished just about everything a baseball player could hope to achieve. He's a five-time All-Star, a four-time Silver Slugger and one of the most recognizable shortstops in Major League Baseball.
But on October 26, Lindor received an honor that has little to do with his numbers at the plate or his performance on the field.
The New York Mets star was named the 2026 recipient of the Roberto Clemente Award, Major League Baseball's highest individual honor for a player's character, philanthropy and community impact.
For Lindor, the recognition carries an additional layer of meaning. He's a proud Puerto Rican native who grew up learning about Clemente, the legendary Hall of Famer whose impact on baseball extended far beyond the diamond.
Now, Lindor joins the group of players whose actions have helped carry that legacy forward.
Francisco Lindor's Roberto Clemente Award Is About More Than Baseball
The Roberto Clemente Award recognizes the MLB player who best represents baseball through community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions on and off the field.
Clemente, a 15-time All-Star and one of baseball's greatest players, died on December 31, 1972, while traveling to deliver humanitarian aid to earthquake victims in Nicaragua.
His commitment to helping others became inseparable from his legacy.
For Lindor, that example began long before he reached the Major Leagues.
Growing up in Puerto Rico, he learned about Clemente's career and humanitarian efforts in school. Lindor has spoken about how Clemente inspired him to use his own platform to help others.
Lindor is the fifth Puerto Rican-born player to win the award, joining Edgar Martínez, Carlos Delgado, Carlos Beltrán and Yadier Molina.
That connection makes this recognition particularly significant. Puerto Rico has a rich baseball tradition, and Clemente remains one of its most influential figures. Lindor's award recognizes not only his individual work but also the continuing influence of a Puerto Rican icon whose example transcends generations.
Lindor's Charity Work Starts With Education
One of the clearest examples of Lindor's philanthropy is his commitment to education.
Since 2020, he has donated more than $1 million to Montverde Academy in Florida, his alma mater, helping fund Lindor Hall, a two-story middle school building featuring science and technology laboratories.
He also established the Francisco Lindor Scholarship Fund to help students who otherwise might not have the financial means to attend the school.
His involvement goes beyond writing checks. Lindor remains engaged with students through mentorship, career guidance and youth baseball initiatives.
That commitment reflects an important part of his charitable work: creating opportunities that can continue to benefit young people long after a particular event or donation.
Giving Back to Puerto Rico
Lindor's connection to his home island has also shaped his response to natural disasters.
Following Hurricanes Maria in 2017 and Fiona in 2022, he provided financial support for relief efforts in Puerto Rico. He has also helped restore athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas and hosted youth baseball clinics.
These efforts connect his philanthropic work to the communities that helped shape him.
For Puerto Rican athletes who reach the highest levels of professional sports, success can provide an opportunity to give back to the places where their journeys began. Lindor has used that opportunity to support recovery efforts, youth development and access to sports.
His work also includes partnerships focused on environmental conservation and ongoing community support.
Making a Difference in Queens
Lindor's impact isn't limited to Puerto Rico or his former school.
In New York, he and his wife, Katia, have supported programs designed to help children and families. Their initiatives include annual back-to-school efforts with New Balance that provide hundreds of students with backpacks and essential school supplies.
Lindor also launched Lindor's Leaders in 2026, a year-long leadership development program for students in Bayside High School's Sports Medicine Program.
The initiative focuses on mental health, communication, teamwork and leadership. Lindor personally mentors participating students, helping them develop skills they can apply in school and throughout their lives.
He has also worked with Children's Miracle Network Hospitals, Special Olympics Florida and organizations supporting youth and families navigating disability.
On the field, Lindor represents the Mets. In the community, his work reaches far beyond the team's fan base.
A $100,000 Boost for the SEEN Foundation
The 2026 award also brings additional support for a cause Lindor and his wife have embraced.
Capital One is donating $100,000 to the SEEN Foundation in honor of Lindor's achievement. The organization works to empower young people, create opportunities and strengthen communities, including supporting families with children navigating physical disabilities.
The contribution gives Lindor's recognition a direct charitable impact, helping support an organization whose mission aligns with the couple's philanthropic efforts.
It's a fitting addition to an award designed not simply to celebrate what a player has done, but to help extend the impact of that work.
Carrying Roberto Clemente's Legacy Forward
There is no shortage of ways to measure Lindor's baseball career. His offensive production, defense, leadership and importance to the Mets will continue to shape how his playing days are remembered.
The Roberto Clemente Award recognizes a different side of that career.
Lindor has invested in education, supported Puerto Rico after devastating hurricanes, mentored students and helped provide opportunities for children and families in New York. These are tangible efforts that extend his influence beyond the ballpark.
His Puerto Rican heritage makes the honor particularly meaningful because Clemente's legacy has long been part of the island's baseball identity. Lindor grew up learning about Clemente's commitment to service, and he now has an opportunity to inspire the next generation in a similar way.
Winning the Roberto Clemente Award is not just another milestone for Francisco Lindor. It's recognition of the person he has chosen to be away from baseball.
For the Mets, Puerto Rico and the broader baseball community, that may be one of his most meaningful accomplishments yet.

item.content:encoded:
New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor has won the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award, Major League Baseball announced.
This award is given annually to the player "who best represents the game of Baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.
Each team nominates one player, similar to the NFL's Walter Payton Man of the Year Award.
Lindor earned the award for his contributions to education, youth leadership and disaster relief in Puerto Rico, according to a league statement. As part of Lindor's winning the award, Capital One will be donating $100,000 to the SEEN Foundation in Lindor's honor. The SEEN Foundation "empowers youth, create opportunities and foster positive community impact" among families dealing with disabilities.
Here are the other charitable efforts the league highlighted in its statement.
- "Lindor's Leaders Program (est. 2026) — Launched in partnership with New Balance, this year-long leadership development initiative for students in Bayside High School's Sports Medicine Program focuses on mental health, communication, teamwork, and leadership. Lindor personally mentors participating students, equipping them with the confidence to lead in their schools and communities.
- Support for Children's Miracle Network Hospitals — In 2026, Francisco partnered with Dairy Queen and Children's Miracle Network Hospitals for Miracle Treat Day, raising critical funds for local children's hospitals by donating directly to families in need $1 or more from every Blizzard Treat sold.
- Transformative Commitment to Education — A proud graduate of Montverde Academy, Lindor has donated more than $1 million since 2020 to build Lindor Hall, a two-story middle school building featuring state-of-the-art science and technology labs. He also established the Francisco Lindor Scholarship Fund to provide financial aid for students, remaining personally involved through mentorship, career guidance, annual PLAY BALL youth events, and equipment donations for the school's baseball team.
- Disaster Relief and Advocacy for Puerto Rico — Deeply committed to his native Puerto Rico, Francisco provided essential financial support following Hurricanes Maria and Fiona, restored athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas, and hosted youth clinics. He continues to partner with organizations including Team Rubicon, the Amazin' Mets Foundation, Players for the Planet, and Rescate Playas Borinquen for ongoing recovery and environmental conservation.
- Serving the Queens Community — Through an annual back-to-school initiative with New Balance, Lindor provides hundreds of students each year with backpacks and essential school supplies. Now in its third season, Lindor Smile Tuesdays welcomes youth organizations to Citi Field for educational experiences promoting dental health, wellness, self-confidence, and mentorship.
- Growing the Game — Passionate about making baseball accessible and inclusive, Francisco regularly participates in the Mets' Clinic for Champions with Special Olympics Florida and hosts the Lindor Clinic for Kids for local youth leagues and Boys & Girls Clubs."
Lindor is the fifth Mets player to win the award. He joins Curtis Granderson (2016), Carlos Delgado (2006), Al Leiter (2000) and Gary Carter (1989).
The most recent winners of the award are Lindor, Mookie Betts, Salvador Perez, Aaron Judge and Justin Turner over the past five seasons.
The award was originally named the Commissioner's Award when it began in 1971. It was renamed the Roberto Clemente Award just two years later for Clemente, who died on New Year's Eve in 1972 while on a flight delivering supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor has won the Roberto Clemente Award from Major League Baseball for his humanitarian work.
Lindor was to receive the award before Game 3 of the World Series on Monday night.
A five-time All-Star, Lindor became the fifth recipient of Puerto Rican descent to receive the award after Edgar Martinez (2004), Carlos Delgado (2006), Carlos Beltrán (2013) and Yadier Molina (2018).
Lindor and his wife Katia have worked with Children’s Miracle Network Hospitals; the SEEN Foundation, a disability advocacy group; Special Olympics Florida; and Boys & Girls Clubs of America.
He donated to relief efforts in Puerto Rico after Hurricanes Maria and Fiona, restoring athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas, and donated more than $1 million to build Lindor Hall at the Montverde Academy, a school he graduated from in Monteverde, Florida.
Lindor launched a leadership development initiative for students in the sports medicine program at Bayside High School in New York; and funded backpacks and school supplies in Queens, the New York City borough where the Mets' Citi Field is located.
Clemente was a 15-time All-Star from Puerto Rico who was killed in a plane crash on New Year’s Eve 1972 while attempting to deliver supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua. The award is given annually to a major league player who represents the sport through character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions on and off the field.

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Trevor Megill was shouting in celebration and the Milwaukee Brewers were bolting out of the dugout to congratulate one another, believing they had just escaped a ninth-inning jam to win Game 1 of the World Series.
Not quite yet.
What initially was ruled a game-ending double play got overturned after a video review showed Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
No problem.
Megill regrouped and struck out Jonny DeLuca with two runners in scoring position as Milwaukee edged the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 on Friday night.
“It’s good to get the first win out of the way,” Megill said. “That’s where all the nerves are at. First game, a lot of anticipation and build-up to where we are right now.”
The ninth inning was particularly nerve-racking for the Brewers and the sellout crowd attending Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982.
“You have a big range of emotions,” said team captain Christian Yelich, whose RBI triple in the first put the Brewers ahead for good. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn’t put a runner on since the sixth until it mounted its comeback attempt against Megill.
Jonathan Aranda, who went 3 for 3 with a walk, and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put runners on second and third before Junior Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Liam Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was called a 4-6-3 double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared. But then the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
“You’ve got to think worst-case scenario there,” Megill said. “I thought the challenge was at first base, maybe a bobble or something. But it was pretty clear once the replay went up that it was on the play at second base. Zoomed in and it didn’t look good. It’s all right. We picked up Cooper there. He’ll pick us up tomorrow.”
The out call at second was changed to safe by umpire Alfonso Márquez at the MLB Replay Center, which caught Pratt by surprise.
“Obviously, it was close,” the 22-year-old rookie said. “I just didn’t think it was enough to overturn, so I wasn’t thinking anything of it. The video I saw, thought my cleat was dragging. … There must have been some other angles that I haven’t seen. It ultimately didn’t matter because we won.”
The Brewers won because Megill got DeLuca to swing and miss at a 2-2 pitch, capping a night in which Tampa Bay went 0 for 6 with runners in scoring position.
“This is an extremely confident group,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “You know that. We know that. They’re going to be fine. I think the frustration comes from we were one swing of the bat away right at the end of potentially taking the lead.”
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
This marks the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
Milwaukee took a 2-0 lead in the first inning against Nick Martinez. NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to help the Brewers stay in front before relievers Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby shut down the Rays through the eighth.
Misiorowski, who had a season-low three strikeouts, opened the game with a 103.5 mph fastball — the fastest pitch ever thrown in a World Series.
“The adrenaline kind of took over, and I tensed up and threw it hard,” said Misiorowski, who earned the win. “Then I settled down, and that was the game plan, to settle in and do me. Don’t try and overdo it.”
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.
Tampa Bay managed to hang around thanks in part to Martinez, who gave up those two runs in the first but held Milwaukee scoreless through the rest of his five-inning stint. The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh when Chourio singled home Pratt.
Then came all the action in the ninth, with the Brewers’ premature celebration followed by a team-wide sigh of relief as Pratt offered some parting words to Megill.
“I just said, ‘Thank you, man. Thanks for picking me up,’” Pratt said. “That’s what this game is. It’s a game of pick-me-up. He picked me up today.”
Up next
Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA) pitches for Tampa Bay and Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47) starts for Milwaukee in Game 2 on Saturday night. In this postseason, Rasmussen is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA and Henderson is 0-0 with a 3.00 ERA.

item.content:encoded:
There were 13 outfield-eligible players worth at least $20 in the FanGraphs Player Rater in 2026, just two fewer than the first base spot. If you remember that you only need to start one first baseman (and potentially a corner infielder and DH) while you might need to start as many as five outfielders at a time, well, you can see why this is problematic.
That's not to say the outfield is somehow a wasteland for Fantasy right now. First base was unusually strong in 2026, but in 2025, there were three times as many $20 players with outfield eligibility as at first base. And it's worth noting that the 13 $20 outfielders in 2026 are actually a few more than 2025's nine.
On the whole, I look at outfield as a position with a decent amount of depth in a three-outfielder, 12-team league. You should be able to draft a full lineup without feeling too bad about your outfield options in that formula.
Once you start getting into five-outfielder leagues, and especially deeper leagues with 15 teams, it starts to feel a lot more thin. That's to be expected, of course, but it's important to keep that in mind when you're preparing for the 2027 season. You don't have to make the position a priority in every draft, but if you aren't cognizant of it, you could end up with a real weakness in those deeper leagues.
For more on the state of the outfield position, .
2026 Outfield Review
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, CHC: .280 - 119 - 45 - 107 - 41
- Yordan Alvarez, HOU: .316 - 105 - 42 - 106 - 1
- Fernando Tatis Jr., SDP: .289 - 96 - 25 - 83 - 38
- Randy Arozarena, SEA: .281 - 113 - 26 - 79 - 26
- Jordan Walker, STL: .269 - 97 - 29 - 102 - 22
- James Wood, WSN: .265 - 106 - 30 - 77 - 21
- Jackson Chourio, MIL: .291 - 96 - 25 - 75 - 23
- Alec Burleson, STL: .279 - 89 - 26 - 116 - 4
- Jake McCarthy, COL: .291 - 80 - 15 - 83 - 32
- Michael Harris II, ATL: .294 - 79 - 26 - 87 - 12
- Jackson Merrill, SDP: .254 - 86 - 26 - 87 - 27
- Bryce Harper, PHI: .269 - 93 - 29 - 87 - 7
- Jake Bauers, MIL: .266 - 93 - 26 - 86 - 11
- Seiya Suzuki, CHC: .270 - 96 - 26 - 86 - 3
- Carson Benge, NYM: .282 - 86 - 20 - 65 - 22
- Andy Pages, LAD: .274 - 75 - 23 - 85 - 13
- Corbin Carroll, ARI: .239 - 91 - 22 - 78 - 21
- Oneil Cruz, PIT: .280 - 65 - 20 - 67 - 30
- Daylen Lile, WSN: .246 - 81 - 22 - 89 - 15
- Jac Caglianone, KCR: .289 - 72 - 23 - 75 - 7
- Bryan Reynolds, PIT: .261 - 102 - 17 - 72 - 9
- Chandler Simpson, TBR: .306 - 66 - 0 - 38 - 46
- Riley Greene, DET: .280 - 79 - 21 - 75 - 3
- Ceddanne Rafaela, BOS: .285 - 67 - 16 - 70 - 17
"Marginal player signs with the Rockies and has a Coors Field-inflated career season" used to be a pretty reliable archetype. Still, the Rockies have given Fantasy players little to get excited about in recent years. Jake McCarthy stands out as a notable exception, as his contact-and-speed profile proved to be a perfect fit for Coos Field. We're talking about relatively easy career-best production across the board, in a way that feels relatively obvious in retrospect. I don't have a ton of faith that this would prove replicable in any other ballpark — the gap between his .321 expected wOBA and his .349 actual mark was the 20th biggest in baseball — but it works there. As long as he isn't traded, McCarthy is a good bet to replicate his 2026 success.
I also want to highlight Harris and Merrill, because it feels very natural to group them together. They're both younger than you might realize – Harris will turn 26 shortly before his sixth MLB season in March, while Merrill won't even be 24 on Opening Day. They're also both linked by the combination of plus athleticism and bat speed, plus pretty poor approaches at the plate. They are, on the whole, capable of overcoming their poor swing decisions with outlier outcomes when they make contact, but that isn't always the case for either. Hence, the lengthy slumps that have held both back in recent years. They both got the good end of their range of outcomes in 2026, and we saw how high the ceiling can be for both. But drafting either for their 2026 outcome will carry inherent risks until they show some growth in their plate discipline.
Biggest Breakout from 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
How could it be anyone else? Crow-Armstrong went from being a talented but deeply flawed hitter to arguably the best player in baseball, and he did it in-season. Early on, he looked more or less like the same guy he had always been, walking just nine times in 128 plate appearances through the end of June; he walked at least 12 times in each of the final five months of the season, something he had never done in any of his previous 13 months. He did that without sacrificing the pull-side power that has long been a key part of his game, and it turned him into one of the most dominant hitters in the game. Expecting all of those gains to carry over into 2027 might be asking a bit much — sometimes guys just get super locked in for a while — but he's clearly a much-improved hitter, and one who should be the first player taken in every single Roto league in 2027. And he shouldn't go much later in points leagues, where he was also the top player in 2026.
Honorable Mention: Jordan Walker, Cardinals
Okay, so if it were going to be anyone but Crow-Armstrong, it would be Walker, who went from being one of the biggest prospect busts in recent seasons to one of the best players in Fantasy. Walker still had pretty bad plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues, but he overcame that by being more aggressive early in the count and by doing more damage when he did make contact. The plate discipline issues and a late-season swoon — his expected wOBA dropped from .374 to .290 from the first half to the second — hint at the kind of risk involved in buying fully into what he did in 2026, and I suspect I'll be a little lower on him than the consensus. On the other hand, those were the exact reasons I cited to avoid Crow-Armstrong before the season, and look how that turned out. There's something to be said for just betting on the young, super-talented players when they show it.
Biggest Bust from 2026
The overall numbers don't show it, but Judge looked more or less like himself before he started dealing with that rib injury. In March and April, he posted a .450 xwOBA, right in line with his typical mark, but then things went downhill even before he ultimately went on the IL with a fractured rib. Was his downturn because of the injury? If so, then I think you can still make the case for him as a top-five pick in any league. But we're talking about a guy who will be 35 early next season, coming off a largely lost season that also came with an apparent decline in the underlying skill level, and that's a lot of red flags to overlook in a top-five pick. I might end up with Judge ranked that way come the spring, but it won't feel good.
Honorable Mention: Kyle Tucker, Dodgers
Maybe you don't think he was worth the contract the Dodgers gave him. Fair enough; you won't be alone in holding that opinion. But anyone who tells you there was any way to see this kind of disaster coming from Tucker is just lying to you. A 29-year-old went out and posted the worst batting average, on-base percentage, and slugging percentage of his career, and in two of those cases, it wasn't even close. Tucker had the combination of bat speed, athleticism, and plate discipline that should protect him against this kind of drop-off. Maybe the lights in L.A. were too bright for him. Maybe the pressure of the contract got to him. But I don't believe Tucker has just completely lost the ability to be an impact player, and he's still in what should be one of the best lineups in baseball, so I'll buy the bounce-back at what should be a steeply discounted price. The fact that he put together an excellent September and a very good postseason run certainly makes that an easier story to tell, of course.
Biggest rankings movers from 2026 to 2027
Up: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs; Yordan Alvarez, Astros; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Jake Bauers, Brewers
As maybe the biggest Yordan Alvarez believer in the entire Fantasy industry coming into 2026, I do worry there's going to be a big overcorrection on him in 2027. We didn't learn anything new about Alvarez. If you think 2026 was a breakout season of some sort for him, I'm sorry, but you just weren't paying attention; he's just always been this good. His .442 xwOBA was higher than his career average, sure, but it was also not even the highest of his career, and he had a separate season with a .436 mark, too. The skills have always been there, but the difference is that he stayed healthy in 2026 after a bunch of injuries in previous seasons. I'm thrilled that he stayed healthy, and the fact that he did it in a season when his standing among Fantasy players was never lower is a good reminder that the Fantasy community isn't nearly as good at predicting who will and won't stay healthy as we think. But that will also be true in 2027: He'll be a top-five pick in most leagues despite the injury risk not being substantially different than it was last season. That's not to say he shouldn't be a top-five pick, of course; it's to say that he should have been a lot closer to a top-five pick last season than he was.
You could make a case for Bauers as the biggest breakout at outfield, because he was viewed as an even bigger afterthought than Walker was. He was a 30-year-old platoon specialist, after all! That he somehow went out in 2026 and put up a .901 OPS against lefties and had the best season of his career by a mile came completely out of nowhere, and it's going to be very interesting to see what the market for him as a free agent looks like this offseason. I buy a lot of what he did in 2026, and I suspect there will be enough skepticism around it to keep his price pretty reasonable. But betting on age-30 breakouts is historically a pretty bad idea, so you'll have to get a pretty big discount on what he did in 2026 to make him worth the risk, I think.
Down: Ronald Acuna, Braves; Kyle Tucker, Dodgers; Wyatt Langford, Rangers; Brent Rooker, Athletics
I wanted to make Langford one of the biggest bust picks, if only to highlight the fact that he has almost certainly been the least profitable pick in Fantasy over the past three years. He has struggled to stay healthy and just hasn't been the impact player you'd expect from a guy who had the kind of prospect pedigree he did — not to mention the benefit of the doubt the Fantasy community has continued to give him. I suspect that will come to an end in 2027, and … it kind of makes me more excited about buying into him this season. Because, for as frustrating and disappointing as he's been as a big-leaguer, his per-162 game pace for his career is pretty terrific: 90 runs, 24 homers, 24 steals, and 77 RBI. If he just does that in 2027, isn't that worth something like a fifth-round pick? And I don't think that's the ceiling for Langford, who has put up those numbers at a very young age while playing through a variety of injuries and has certainly flashed a higher ceiling at times. I'm not trying to excuse his poor performance; I'm just pointing out that all he has to do is stay healthy to be a very good Fantasy option. That's usually a good player to buy into at a discount.
The notoriously frugal A's are surely feeling some degree of buyer's remorse on Rooker's contract, but that contract should assure that he continues to play every day for them. His disappointing season came to an end after just 48 games, but he was on pace for another 30-homer season despite the injury. The .200 average is a tough look, as was the career-worst 32% strikeout rate, and the big drop off as a 31-year-old will rightly lead to plenty of skepticism around the potential of a bounce back. But that will also mean Rooker will come at a huge discount, potentially with a price outside the top 200 in many drafts. I'll buy that dip, personally. If you can buy him as a very cheap bench bat, there's no downside.
Offseason preview
Who needs an upgrade most?
A bunch of these teams are straddling the line between trying to go for it and needing to rebuild. The Reds could very well be in the market for a big upgrade in the outfield, or they could decide to move Elly De La Cruz and hit the reset button (again). The Astros could decide to give it one more run with this core, or they could move Alvarez and pivot to the future. The Phillies seem most likely to try to take a big swing, if only because Dave Dombrowski only knows how to take big swings. However, the Cardinals loom as a team that is ascending and could decide to get involved in the free-agent market with their core of cost-controlled position players.
Top impending free agents
- Randy Arozarena
- Seiya Suzuki
- Ian Happ
- Jake Bauers
- Trent Grisham
- Daulton Varsho
- Luis Robert
- Ramon Laureano
- George Springer
Arozarena is such a fascinating free agent. He's coming off a perfectly timed career-best season, but he'll be 32 before Opening Day and has rated out as a pretty terrible defender for several years running. There's probably no chance he gets anything more than a five-year contract in free agency, and he might need to agree to a move to DH as soon as 2027, two things that might be a tough pill to swallow. But having the best season of his career in the toughest offensive environment in baseball is no small thing, and nobody can deny his flair for the dramatic would be a great fit for a team with championship aspirations. The underlying skill set doesn't look so different from previous seasons, but his price will likely be higher than ever, making him one of the more obvious players to avoid in drafts for 2027, no matter where he lands.
Suzuki and, to a lesser extent, Happ look like players who will carry pretty solid value in Fantasy no matter where they land, but everyone else looks pretty context-dependent. Varsho's pull-heavy swing (and elite center field defense) would be a perfect fit for the Yankees, for example, but would be a much less interesting profile elsewhere. Stay tuned.
Trade candidates 
- Yordan Alvarez, Astros
- Jarren Duran, Red Sox
- Steven Kwan, Guardians
- Byron Buxton, Twins
- Brent Rooker, Athletics
- Jake McCarthy, Rockies
Alvarez feels like the biggest wild card here. The Astros won the AL West, but with just a .500 record, and they had such a poor showing in a two-game Wild Card round loss to the White Sox that the hometown crowd showered them with boos along the way. The Astros have lost their long-held edge over the competition, and while Alvarez's contract isn't expiring, he only has two years left on a relatively below-market deal. So this might be their last chance to maximize their return for him. The Astros are in flux in a lot of ways after firing Dana Brown, so they might not be positioned to make a big, franchise-altering move, but they would probably be best served trying to get off the treadmill of mediocrity sooner rather than later.
It increasingly looks like the Red Sox should have traded Duran at least a year ago, if not longer. All of a sudden, he's a 30-year-old corner outfielder who probably shouldn't play every day against lefties, and while he'll likely still earn a below-market salary in arbitration, he no longer looks like a real bargain. His skill set still has plenty of value for Fantasy (20 homers, 21 steals will always play), and I'd bet on him improving on last year's .207 average, but this isn't an early-round profile anymore.
Top rookies to know for 2026
- Josue De Paula, Dodgers
- Walker Jenkins, Twins
- Eduardo Quintero, Dodgers
- Theo Gillen, Rays
- Mike Sirota, Dodgers
- Zyhir Hope, Tigers
- Edward Florentino, Pirates
- Eric Hartman, Braves
- Drew Burress, Athletics
- Josiah Hartshorn, Cubs
- Lazaro Montes, Mariners
Jenkins is probably the most likely player here to be in an Opening Day lineup – I'm not sure what would have to happen for him not to be there, absent injury. He didn't take the league by storm in his first 26 games, but he was actually pretty great once he got adjusted, hitting .385/.400/.615 with just three strikeouts over his final 10 games. He has power, speed, and an excellent approach at the plate and should be a popular breakout candidate for 2027.
But not as popular as De Paula could be. I say "could" because, well, there's no obvious place for him to play. It's definitely not going to be in right field or DH, and slotting De Paula in at left field would require finding somewhere for Teoscar Hernandez and his large salary to go. Center field is the biggest hole in the Yankees outfield, but De Paula hasn't played there since 2023, and … well, you see the problem here. De Paula destroyed Double-A and very much passed the eye test in 11 MLB games, earning not-totally-unfair comparisons to Juan Soto and Yordan Alvarez for his approach at the plate. He could be an absolute star, but given the roster crunch and the fact that he's only 21 and hasn't played at Triple-A yet, this might be a situation like Junior Caminero's a few years back – remember, he debuted toward the end of the 2023 season but wasn't an everyday player until August of 2024. I hope it doesn't take that long, but we'll have to at least consider the possibility that it will.

item.title: [mlb.com] Rays-Brewers World Series position-by-position breakdown
item.dc:creator: Mike Petriello

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to a most fantastically interesting World Series, in which focusing on the size of the markets involved completely misses the forest for the trees. It’s a No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchup, just the sixth time in the past 30 years that’s happened. It’s a pair of fanbases who have never won before, which marks the first time since 1980 (Royals vs. Phillies) that’s happened, and thus only the second time in more than a century, since the previous time had been 1920.
It’s a matchup of teams that have more than a few connections. Note that Tampa Bay’s top two starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, each came up with Milwaukee, and were teammates on the 2020-21 Brewers. Note, also, that NLCS MVP Jake Bauers made his debut with Tampa Bay back in 2018, and that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold spent nine years in the Tampa Bay front office before moving to Wisconsin.
It's more than just that. Depending on how you view your baseball aesthetics, it's a delightfully throwback sort of on-field style. It’s not that these teams eschew analytical thinking -- exactly the opposite, really -- but no team struck out less than the Rays, each team finished in the top five in steals and the bottom 10 in homers, and the bunt hits leaderboard goes “Tampa Bay first, Milwaukee second.”
Throw in a pair of excellent defenses, and you know what you’re going to get here, which is excellent baseball played by a pair of teams that actually look a whole lot like one another. We know what else we're going to get, too: an incredibly interesting series. Which side has the edge?
Catcher
William Contreras, over the past five years, has a pretty solid argument to make as being the best all-around catcher in the National League. While his bat over the last two seasons (110 OPS+) isn’t quite what it was at his peak from 2022-24 (129 OPS+), it’s reliably solid, and then of course he’s been fantastic in eight playoff games, posting a 1.157 OPS with three homers. It’s hard to overstate how important the midseason acquisition of Liam Hicks (129 OPS+ in 41 games for Tampa Bay) was, really helping to lengthen a top-heavy lineup, though he hasn’t done much with the bat in the playoffs. Given relatively similar defensive value, we’ll give a small edge based on track record.
Advantage: Brewers
First base
It's a tale of two winding paths here, as Jonathan Aranda finally had his breakout last season, a decade after he signed as an amateur free agent with Tampa Bay, and of course Jake Bauers' long road to get to this point has been well-chronicled. Bauers has the offensive edge both in terms of power and getting on base, and neither are terribly strong defensive players, so given the mild 2026 regular-season advantage and also the superior performance in October, it’s hard not to choose Bauers on this. Great stories, both.
Advantage: Brewers
Second base
Brice Turang is the best all-around second baseman in the game, pairing excellent defense with a more recently found power stroke, popping 21 homers and driving in 100. The Rays have certainly found some ways to get value out of their second-base duo of Richie Palacios and Ben Williamson, but it’s a relatively below-average spot for Tampa Bay and, either way, we’re comparing to Milwaukee’s best-in-class superstar. This one is probably the biggest mismatch of any pairing on the list.
Advantage: Brewers
Shortstop
Here’s how you know how well-regarded Taylor Walls is on defense: The Rays continue to play him every day despite a near-total lack of offense from the position, as he’s posted all of a .381 OPS this month, and even that was juiced a little by the inexplicable three walks that Cleveland issued him in ALCS Game 6. It’s not just a small-sample thing, either, as Walls has been a routinely ineffective hitter for the entirety of his career.
There’s no doubt that Milwaukee’s Cooper Pratt is a stronger offensive force, though that’s been more good than great, with a league-average line as a rookie and a mostly singles-based approach in the playoffs. While he’s expected to be a quality shortstop as his career progresses, a number of important miscues in the postseason tilt this one to the more surehanded Walls.
Advantage: Rays
Third base
If there’s some argument that this series features more depth than true superstars, then that case falls apart a little at third, where Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero posted his second consecutive 40-plus homer season on his way to, most likely, some high placement on AL MVP ballots. It’s true that prior to his ALCS Game 6 homer, his bat had been relatively quiet in October, but we’re also talking about all of eight games against some of the best pitching the sport has to offer. (The average fastball he’s seen? 96.8 mph.) There’s an obvious speed-and-defense edge for Milwaukee in David Hamilton and Joey Ortiz, but not quite so much that you’d take either or both over Caminero, or that it’s really close at all.
Advantage: Rays
Left field
This is actually the most fun comparison, because who do you like more, the 22-year-old power-and-defense superstar in Jackson Chourio -- the only player in history to have three 20-20 seasons through age-22 -- or the 25-year-old elite speed-and-contact guy in Chandler Simpson, who improved his defense to the point that both were named Gold Glove finalists last week? It’s yet another reminder that there’s more than one way to provide value, and certainly both teams are very pleased with their situations here. It’s hard, though, not to default to Chourio, who might already be a top-20 position player in the sport. If both can run and field, and only one has any power, then the advantage writes itself.
Advantage: Brewers
Center field
In Garrett Mitchell and Jonny DeLuca, you have two very strong defensive center fielders, though you’d probably give the slight edge here to DeLuca. (Cedric Mullins also carries a good glove, though this spot has belonged to DeLuca all month.) The question about their bats is what shape of production you prefer, in that Mitchell struck out considerably more than DeLuca, but he also had an on-base percentage 54 points higher, thanks in large part to a walk rate three times as high. While we’re not weighing postseason performance too much here, it’s worth noting that Mitchell has had some huge hits, while DeLuca mostly has not. This is about as razor-thin as we’ll see here, but even if Mitchell’s glove isn’t as good, it’s still good, and he gets on base. Edge, Milwaukee. A small one, anyway.
Advantage: Brewers
Right field
For everything that Sal Frelick has done for the Brewers over his four seasons with the team -- and he has done quite a bit -- this was not a terribly strong season for him, posting a career-worst 70 OPS+, and he’s managed only three singles and a few walks in the playoffs. That’s not to say that he can’t help the team win in other ways, because he can and does, but Tampa Bay’s Victor Mesa Jr. has been one of the team’s breakout stars, putting up not only a 127 OPS+ but also some truly elite defensive metrics, in just half a season. You’re already familiar, anyway, with his absolute cannon of a throwing arm. Mesa Jr. wasn’t on the Opening Day roster and didn’t even join the Rays for good until late May. He might just be one of the most important players in the World Series, though.
Advantage: Rays
Designated hitter
It would be hard to find two players who mean more to their respective teams than veterans Yandy Díaz (in his eighth season with Tampa Bay) and recently appointed Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich (in his ninth season as a Brewer). Neither plays the field much anymore, nor is either at or near their peak of offensive performance these days. But Díaz far outperformed Yelich during the regular season (124 OPS+ to 91 OPS+, where again, 100 is average), and that’s held true in the postseason, too, where Yelich has been held out of certain games against tough lefties in favor of Andrew Vaughn. At DH, literally the only thing that matters is “dangerous bat,” and that’s Díaz still, after all these years.
Advantage: Rays
Starting pitchers
If we’re talking about each team’s top three starters, which represent the bulk of a postseason rotation, then it’s Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser for Milwaukee, and Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez for Tampa Bay. Those six pitchers, so far in the playoffs, have combined for a 1.87 ERA. They’re not that good, obviously, with every underlying metric saying that the strikeout rate has been just average, and that they’ve been bailed out to some extent by excellent defense and relief pitching.
Still: When Misiorowski -- the presumptive NL Cy Young winner, the most dominant per-batter pitcher of the moment -- has the highest postseason ERA of these six, you know how strong each team is here. You really can’t look at full-season stats, either, because it goes without saying that the Tampa Bay version of Peralta is a very different pitcher than New York version we saw prior to the Trade Deadline. Misiorowski is the best of the six, but is he that much better than Rasmussen right now, himself an ace? Maybe not.
These are two strengths, but we like Tampa Bay ever so slightly more for one reason: depth. No Milwaukee starter, not even the top ones, has managed to get past five innings in the playoffs so far, which puts a lot of pressure on the bullpens. (There’s a particularly interesting angle here if Tampa Bay’s high-contact, flat-swing hitters can foul off enough Misiorowski pitches to wear him out, as has already happened to him this month.) If you look past the top three, you’d probably take Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour to get outs a little more than Milwaukee’s Shane Drohan and Dustin May.
They’re both good, obviously. They’re World Series starting rotations. We’d give the ever-so-slight edge to Tampa Bay in a best of seven.
Advantage: Rays
Relief pitchers
If Milwaukee’s starters have been more good than great this month, then their relievers have more than picked up the slack, as you’ve almost certainly heard the note that in 40 2/3 postseason innings, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed all of six earned runs. While most of the focus there lands on Aaron Ashby or closer Trevor Megill, realize that JoJo Romero has a 47% strikeout rate this month, and that Abner Uribe, Antonio Senzatela, Megill and Ashby are all averaging more than 98 mph on their heaters this month. In fact, it is the second-hardest-throwing bullpen of the pitch tracking era (since 2008) -- at 98 mph even -- and the hardest that doesn’t include Mason Miller.
It makes, then, for an ironic matchup against a Tampa Bay bullpen that is A) also very good but B) does not throw hard, comparatively, at just 93.2 mph. (That goes down slightly, if you don't include Peralta’s impressive appearance in ALCS Game 4.) Much depends on the status of Bryan Baker, their All-Star closer, who was used so heavily against Cleveland that his fastball, which averaged 96.3 mph during the regular season, sunk below 93 mph in ALCS Game 6.
He was still good, of course. All the Rays are. It’s just hard not to go with Milwaukee, given their superior depth and full rest.
Advantage: Brewers
Prediction
It should be clear by now that this is an incredibly tightly matched series between two mirror-image teams, the best in their respective leagues, and you could as easily claim “rust or rest” for Milwaukee after their layoff, no matter which narrative you’d like to go with. Milwaukee has the biggest-name pitcher in Misiorowski; Tampa Bay has clearly the biggest star hitter in Caminero; and both sides play strong defense and win in ways that aren’t just waiting for the homer.
We like that Milwaukee has the home-field advantage, and the bullpen edge, and also that their lineup just seems a little deeper; in the second half of the season, no team -- not the Dodgers, not the Cubs, not anyone -- got more production from the No. 6 through 9 spots in their lineup than Milwaukee. That’s in part because of the middle infield, where the Brewers were third best, while Tampa Bay was third weakest. There’s at least some question about what shape Baker will be in, though three days of rest before the World Series ought to help.
It won’t be a cakewalk, because there’s too much talent and similarity on both sides for that. But every small edge matters, and Milwaukee has enough of them that we expect the second World Series title in city history, and the first for the Brewers franchise. Get ready to slide, Bernie.
Brewers in seven.

item.title: [NBC Sports] Early 2027 Fantasy Baseball Starting Pitcher Rankings: How far do Paul Skenes and Hunter Brown fall?
item.dc:creator: Eric Samulski
item.description: The World Series is about to begin, and we’re being treated to a doozy of a series between the Brewers and the Rays. However, for the 28 other teams, they are turning their attention to 2027, so we’ll join them in that for a bit with some starting pitcher rankings for next season. This is now my fourth year publishing my starting pitcher rankings and my second year doing it this early. In many ways, I like doing a first pass at rankings this year. At this point, it’s hard to overthink. Most play
item.content:encoded:
The World Series is about to begin, and we’re being treated to a doozy of a series between the Brewers and the Rays. However, for the 28 other teams, they are turning their attention to 2027, so we’ll join them in that for a bit with some starting pitcher rankings for next season.
This is now my fourth year publishing my starting pitcher rankings and my second year doing it this early. In many ways, I like doing a first pass at rankings this year. At this point, it’s hard to overthink. Most players aren’t playing games or posting videos of new pitches, so there is nothing to get geeked about. Instead, these rankings are more “gut feel” rankings based on how I feel about all of these pitchers at the end of the season. While I tried not to get too in the weeds about stats, I did look back at the general profile that allowed a pitcher to finish among the top 30 overall starters in recent years, and tried to prioritize pitchers who fit that profile, which mostly meant elevating pitchers who get swings and misses, and penalizing pitchers who don’t seem like a good bet for a full season of innings.
As always, the pitchers are split into tiers based on their skillset or what they’ll provide your fantasy team. The tiers themselves are more important than the rankings inside the tiers, so I wouldn’t split hairs over a few spots in the rankings. I’ve also ranked these pitchers as if I’m doing a 12-team league, so safe but boring low-end starters take a hit in value, etc. I won’t have really long write-ups here, but I’ll be back with updated rankings after the new year, where we can get a little more into the nitty-gritty of the rankings.
OK? Ok, so let’s get started.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Starting Pitcher Rankings
| Rank | Player | Team | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| Aces | | | | |
| 1 | Jacob Misiorowski | MIL | No | Aces |
| 2 | Tarik Skubal | Free Agent | No | Aces |
| 3 | Cam Schlittler | NYY | No | Aces |
| 4 | Cristopher Sánchez | PHI | No | Aces |
| 5 | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | LAD | No | Aces |
There’s not much to discuss about these aces. All five posted a K-BB% of at least 21%, and four of them carried a Stuff+ of 113 or higher. They seem like the clear top five starters in baseball, if they can remain healthy.
| Fringe Young Aces | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 6 | Chase Burns | CIN | No | Young power arms |
| 7 | Payton Tolle | BOS | No | Young power arms |
| 8 | Logan Gilbert | SEA | No | Strikeout guys |
| 9 | Paul Skenes | PIT | No - Maybe? | Young power arms |
There’s an argument to be made for all of these guys being aces. Obviously, Paul Skenes is the key name because he was an ace coming into last season and then posted a
3.82 ERA with a 3.34 SIERA. His Stuff+ also fell from 110 in 2025 to 99 this past season, and he didn’t look fully healthy. Still, he’s one year removed from a 1.97 ERA over 187 IP and was the best young arm in baseball. It’s hard to completely ignore 2024 and 2025. All four of these guys finished with a K-BB% between 20% and 22%, and all are power-first pitchers. Chase Burns threw 154.1 IP with a 2.86 ERA, 3.46 SIERA, 14.4% SwStr%, and 112 Stuff+, and I think that innings number will rise, which will give him even more value. Payton Tolle’s first full season was 148.2 IP with a 3.03 ERA, 21.7% K-BB, and 115 Stuff+. Like Burns, I also expect his innings to rise and his value to tick up.
| Aces With Injury Risk | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 10 | Chris Sale | ATL | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 11 | Garrett Crochet | BOS | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 12 | Jacob deGrom | TEX | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 13 | Zack Wheeler | PHI | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 14 | Bryan Woo | SEA | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 15 | Jesús Luzardo | PHI | No | Elite vets, health risk |
| 16 | Dylan Cease | TOR | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
If you wanted to take any of these starters over the guys in the tier above, that wouldn’t be crazy. They’re not down in this tier because they’re worse pitchers; they’re in this tier because they carry more injury risk than the pitchers in the tier above, and injury risk with your ace is a serious gamble. Chris Sale and Jacob deGrom have been healthy the last two years, but have a lengthy injury history, while Garrett Crochet missed essentially the entire year with an injury, and Dylan Cease saw his velocity plummet at the end of the season and then ended the year on the IL with a shoulder injury. You draft this group for ace outcomes at a price that already reflects the innings risk.
| Ace Upside - Limited Track Record | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 17 | Drew Rasmussen | TBR | No (Previous Risk) | WHIP guys |
| 18 | Cade Cavalli | WSN | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 19 | Braxton Ashcraft | PIT | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 20 | Logan Henderson | MIL | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 21 | Gavin Williams | CLE | No | Rising arms, unproven |
Almost everyone here has one strong season to point to, which is why the tier name fits. Of course, Drew Rasmussen has more than one good season, but he also has had three elbow surgeries and has only pitched over 150 innings once in his MLB career. That prevents me from drafting him where I think his talent should have him because he carries so much extra risk. Cade Cavalli and Logan Henderson also have injury track records that make me a little bit concerned about their durability, and Cavalli’s breakout 2026 season was so closely tied to a velocity increase that I’m just not sure if I want to fully ignore the first three months of the season for him, which were pretty inconsistent. This feels like a fair hedge on the bets for Cavalli. Gavin Williams arguably has the best skills of the group (2.95 SIERA, 25.1% K-BB, 15% SwStr%), but he also had a 3.76 ERA because he is prone to losing his command for an inning in basically every outing.
| High-End SP2 Without Elite K% | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 22 | Parker Messick | CLE | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 23 | Max Fried | NYY | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
| 24 | Griffin Jax | TBR | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 25 | Hunter Brown | HOU | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
These four are valuable because of ERA and WHIP, not big strikeout totals. Parker Messick had moments where he looked like a fantasy ace, but he has just a 97 Stuff+ and his strikeout rate is not the same as the guys in the tier above. Max Fried had another solid season, but his fantasy finishes over the last four years have been super inconsistent because he seems to always miss time with an injury. Hunter Brown was clearly hurt and not pitching well this season, but his strikeout numbers also fell off a cliff in the second half of last season, so I’m not sure we can really rely on him for strikeouts. Griffin Jax is an interesting bet because he only moved into the rotation in the middle of the season, but he had 103.1 innings as a starter and registered a 3.14 ERA, 18.8% K-BB, and 13.6% SwStr%. That’s pretty damn good.
| There’s an Ace in There Somewhere | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 26 | Joe Ryan | MIN | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 27 | Jared Jones | PIT | Yes | Rising arms, unproven |
| 28 | Reid Detmers | LAA | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 29 | Blake Snell | LAD | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 30 | Shohei Ohtani | LAD | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 31 | Carlos Rodón | NYY | Yes | Power arms, command concern |
| 32 | Nolan McLean | NYM | No | Young power arms |
| 33 | Eury Pérez | MIA | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 34 | Emmet Sheehan | LAD | No | Rising arms, unproven |
This tier is a bet on ceiling, and the group has the skills to justify it, but not the track record of consistent production. Obviously, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani, and Carlos Rodon are all in here because of injury concerns that prevent me from giving them enough innings to have them qualify as an ace. Reid Detmers finally had his breakout year in 185.0 innings with a 3.36 ERA and 22.0% K-BB, and Jared Jones shook the rust after his return from injury and pitched 101.2 innings with a 3.28 SIERA and 22.2% K-BB. He really came on at the end of the season. We also still see enough strikeout upside and raw, natural ability from Nolan McLean, Eury Perez, and Emmet Sheehan to have them here. I do worry that McLean had just a 9.6% swinging strike rate, and there may not be as much strikeout upside as people want to believe. This is the range that Misiorowski and Schlittler were going last year, and somebody in here is going to make that jump.
| No Longer Aces, But Safe Floor | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 35 | Gerrit Cole | NYY | No | Strikeout guys |
| 36 | Sonny Gray | BOS | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 37 | Shota Imanaga | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 38 | Logan Webb | SFG | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 39 | Freddy Peralta | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 40 | Sandy Alcantara | MIA | No | Weak contact and durability |
The pitchers here have a long record of quality, and the case for them is volume and ratios. Sandy Alcantara is probably the weakest of the bunch, but he threw 211 innings this season, and we’re back to getting that bulk production from him; a 4.24 SIERA is just not ideal. Freddy Peralta has turned his season around with the Rays, and we’ve seen him be a good starting pitcher for too long to not assume he can continue to pitch well in 2027.
| Fun Upside With Volatility | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 41 | Ian Seymour | TBR | No | Strikeout guys |
| 42 | Andrew Painter | PHI | No | Strikeout guys |
| 43 | Christian Scott | NYM | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 44 | Kade Anderson | SEA | No | Top prospects, clear 2027 job |
| 45 | Kaima Taira | Intl (NPB) | No | International, unproven |
| 46 | Walbert Ureña | LAA | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
The appeal here is strikeout ability, and the risk is large, which is why they’re all down in this range. Ian Seymour flashed the best MLB skills in the tier. In 77 innings as a starter this season, he posted a 2.84 SIERA, 26.7% K-BB, and 14.4% SwStr%. I know the 4.44 ERA wasn’t tremendous, but I believe in the underlying skill set here. Andrew Painter made some key pitch mix changes in the second half of the season that I really like, but, much like Cavalli, his ability to hold velocity will be crucial. Walbert Ureña is confusing. He throws hard and has a nasty changeup plus a sweeper that flashed the ability to miss bats this season. You watch him pitch, and you see a potential stud. But his four-seamer is pretty average, and his 4.14 SIERA and 12.3% K-BB% say he got lucky this season.
The two biggest wild cards here are Kade Anderson and Kaima Taira. Anderson was the top pitching prospect in baseball, but he relies on command and movement over velocity and raw stuff, so it remains to be seen how that translates at the big league level. Taira is almost certain to come over from Japan this offseason after pitching to a 1.36 ERA and 0.97 WHIP with 134 K and 44 BB over 139 IP in NPB this year. We’ve heard he touches 100 mph, has an eight-pitch mix, and could be the best pitching free agent this offseason, other than Skubal.
| Boring But It Can Work | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 47 | Kevin Gausman | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 48 | Aaron Nola | PHI | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 49 | George Kirby | SEA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
All of these guys had pretty gross ERAs but underlying metrics that say they pitched better than the results. We just have to decide if we believe that or not. Aaron Nola made some pitch mix changes in the second half (limiting elevated fastballs) that helped him to produce better results, but George Kirby simply never got it going this year. The draft case for each of these guys is innings, a discounted price based on ERA over SIERA, and a decent chance of a bounce-back, with Kevin Gausman the safest of the three, depending on where he signs.
| Hurt But Should Be Healthy Opening Day | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 50 | Nathan Eovaldi | Free Agent | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 51 | Shane McClanahan | TBR | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 52 | Max Meyer | MIA | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 53 | Ryan Weathers | NYY | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 54 | Ryan Pepiot | TBR | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 55 | Pablo López | MIN | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
| 56 | Nick Pivetta | SDP | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 57 | Corbin Burnes | ARI | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
| 58 | Tyler Glasnow | LAD | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
This is another tier of injuries. These guys ended the season hurt or were hurt for basically the entire year. However, all of them seem likely to begin the year healthy and on the mound for their respective teams. You’re drafting them if the injury discount leaves a bigger gap than the missed time justifies.
| Is There a Next Step? | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 59 | Jackson Jobe | DET | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 60 | Didier Fuentes | ATL | No | Strikeout guys |
| 61 | Trey Yesavage | TOR | Yes | Power arms, command concern |
| 62 | Roki Sasaki | LAD | No | Young power arms |
| 63 | Taj Bradley | MIN | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 64 | Sean Burke | CHW | No | Strikeout guys |
| 65 | Nick Lodolo | CIN | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 66 | River Ryan | DET | Yes | Top prospects, clear 2027 job |
These pitchers have flashed the physical tools, but the consistent results are not there yet. Roki Sasaki, Taj Bradley, and Sean Burke all had stretches in 2026 where they showed clear improvement from 2025. But those stretches didn’t last. Can we count of them in 2027? Trey Yesavage and Jackson Jobe both spent most of the year recovering from injury, but they are top pitching prospects who have shown upside when on the mound. Didier Fuentes was lights out in relief for Atlanta and should get a chance to start, and River Ryan figures to be in the rotation for the Tigers after being the headliner in the Skubal deal. He has flashed real ability before, but he needs to stay healthy.
| More About Command or Weak Contact | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 67 | Trevor Rogers | Free Agent | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 68 | Troy Melton | DET | No | WHIP guys |
| 69 | Sean Manaea | NYM | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 70 | Michael King | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 71 | Framber Valdez | DET | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 72 | Foster Griffin | Free Agent | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 73 | Emerson Hancock | SEA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 74 | Jake Bennett | BOS | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 75 | Tyler Mahle | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 76 | Ranger Suarez | BOS | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 77 | Michael Wacha | KCR | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
These pitchers win with walks and contact, not strikeouts, and many have a Stuff+ under 100 (Tyler Mahle 88, Jake Bennett 93, Ranger Suarez 94, Michael King 95). Some of these guys have been top 30 pitchers before and potentially could again, but the ceiling just doesn’t feel overly high. I would draft this group for innings and WHIP, especially in deeper formats.
| Inconsistent But Has Flashed | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 78 | Robert Gasser | MIL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 78 | MacKenzie Gore | TEX | No | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 79 | José Soriano | TOR | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 80 | Joey Cantillo | CLE | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 81 | Will Warren | NYY | No | Young power arms |
| 82 | Tanner Bibee | CLE | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 83 | Connelly Early | WAS | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 84 | Bryce Miller | SEA | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 85 | Andrew Abbott | CIN | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
Every pitcher here has had a good stretch, but none has strung together a full good year. Some of that is due to injury (Bryce Miller and Connelly Early), but there is just a lot of volatility in this group. Even pitchers that have had good full seasons, like Andrew Abbott, have seemingly never had the profile to back up that success. I do like guys like Early, Miller, Joey Cantillo, or MacKenzie Gore as late-round flyers just in case they can ever put it together or stay healthy.
| Could be a Stud, Could be Demoted | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 87 | Ryan Sloan | SEA | No | Depth prospects, unproven |
| 88 | Hagen Smith | CHW | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 89 | Brandon Sproat | MIL | No | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 90 | Connor Prielipp | MIN | No | Strikeout guys |
| 91 | Shane Drohan | MIL | No | Strikeout guys |
| 92 | Reese Olson | DET | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 93 | Jack Leiter | TEX | Yes | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 94 | Zebby Matthews | MIN | No | Strikeout guys |
This tier is about uncertainty, and it mixes prospects with young arms who have not settled in. Hagen Smith may be the most interesting. He made his MLB debut as a reliever with a 1.32 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 37.4% K, 23.4% K-BB, 2.97 SIERA, 14.6% SwStr%, and 108 Stuff+ over 27.1 IP. However, his Triple-A stats were not as good, and he has some major command concerns. Treat this tier as late-round upside.
| Low Upside But a Safe Floor | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 95 | Shane Baz | BAL | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 96 | Merrill Kelly | ARI | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 97 | Matthew Boyd | CHC | No | WHIP guys |
| 98 | Kyle Leahy | STL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 99 | Michael Soroka | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 100 | Noah Cameron | KCR | No | WHIP guys |
| 101 | Peter Lambert | HOU | No | Strikeout guys |
| 102 | Justin Wrobleski | LAD | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 103 | Brandon Pfaadt | ARI | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 104 | Dean Kremer | MIN | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 105 | Ryne Nelson | ARI | No | Strikeout guys |
| 106 | Cody Bradford | TEX | No | WHIP guys |
| 107 | Casey Mize | Free Agent | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 108 | Andre Pallante | STL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
Most of these pitchers will not win you a league, but they are likely to produce solid ratios and good innings totals. Most of these guys feel like streamers or solid targets in 15-team leagues and draft-and-hold formats.
| No Idea What You Are | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 109 | Luis Castillo | CHW | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 110 | Dustin May | Free Agent | No | Strikeout guys |
| 111 | Anthony Kay | CHW | No | Young power arms |
| 112 | Tatsuya Imai | HOU | No | Strikeout guys |
| 113 | Landen Roupp | SFG | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 114 | Matthew Liberatore | STL | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 115 | Jacob Lopez | ATH | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 116 | Janson Junk | MIA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 117 | Brayan Bello | BOS | No | Weak contact and durability |
I think the title of this group kind of says it all. I have no idea what to make of most of these guys. Matthew Liberatore had an intriguing stretch in the second half. Janson Junk has a deep pitch mix and a solid Stuff+ grade. Brayan Bello looked like an entirely different pitcher when he moved into the bulk reliever role. I was high on Landen Roupp for much of last year, but the results never came. Maybe we need to see something in spring from this group, or maybe we avoid.
| Are You Healthy? I’m Interested If Yes | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 118 | Kyle Harrison | MIL | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 119 | Justin Steele | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 120 | Cade Horton | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 121 | Kris Bubic | Free Agent | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 122 | Edward Cabrera | CHC | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 123 | Jack Flaherty | Free Agent | Yes | Flagged, but pitched in 2026 |
| 124 | Clarke Schmidt | NYY | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 125 | Luis Gil | NYY | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 126 | Tylor Megill | NYM | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 127 | AJ Smith-Shawver | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
All ten of these arms have an injury discount, and the question heading into your fantasy drafts is whether the production will be there when they return. As of now, I can’t draft any of them as more than a late-round dart throw.
| Young Arms But Might Have Rotation Spots | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 128 | Gage Jump | ATH | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 129 | Quinn Mathews | STL | No | Unclassified |
| 130 | David Sandlin | CHW | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 131 | Jonah Tong | NYM | No | Prospects, command concern |
