item.content:encoded:
First pitch for the Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays game is set for 8 p.m. ET on Monday, October 19 at Tropicana Field.
The Rays lead 3-2 in the American League Championship Series after defeating the Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 on Sunday. Tampa Bay can clinch a World Series berth with another win, while the Guardians need a road victory to force a decisive Game 7.
Freddy Peralta takes the mound for the Rays after delivering 6.0 scoreless innings against Cleveland in Game 2. The Guardians, meanwhile, face a challenging pitching situation after using their bullpen for 7.0 innings in Sunday's loss.
Below, we'll break down our Guardians vs. Rays prediction and picks for Monday's ALCS Game 6, including the winner and player picks for PrizePicks.
{{mlb_offer_banner="/style-system/ui-components-playbook"}}
Guardians vs. Rays Prediction, Spread, Over/Under for ALCS Game 6 – Monday, October 19
Tampa Bay enters Game 6 as the home favorites against the Guardians, returning a 1.63x payout if they win outright.
Here are the full payouts for the Guardians vs. Rays game on PrizePicks.
Team Picks data is live at the time of writing and is subject to change.
Peralta (0.79 ERA since August 26) will take the ball for Tampa Bay after delivering one of his best postseason performances in Game 2. The right-hander allowed just 4 hits and 2 walks while striking out 6, relying heavily on his four-seam fastball to overwhelm the Guardians.
Peralta (4.37 season xFIP) has been excellent since joining the Rays, going 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA. He's carried that momentum into October, allowing just a run over 10.2 postseason innings while recording 9 strikeouts.
He's rediscovered some of his early-career velocity, touching 99 MPH with his fastball in his last start.
Shawn Armstrong (2.35 postseason ERA) will open for Cleveland, with the Guardians facing elimination. The right-hander has been outstanding this October, allowing just 2 hits, recording 6 strikeouts, and issuing no walks over 7.2 scoreless innings.
However, Monday will mark his third appearance in as many days after he threw 1.1 scoreless innings in Game 5 and another scoreless frame in Game 4.
Cleveland will need significant bullpen contributions today. Regular-season starters SP Tanner Bibee and SP Joey Cantillo can provide length, while RP Hunter Gaddis, RP Erik Sabrowski, RP Tim Herrin, and closer Cade Smith could all factor in during the later innings.
One thing to note: SP Gavin Williams is unavailable on short rest after throwing 5.0 innings in Game 3, leaving the Guardians without their preferred starter in a must-win situation.
Cleveland's pitching staff must contain a Tampa Bay offense that's scored 10 runs over its last two games. The Guardians' relievers have performed well, but asking Armstrong to open for a third consecutive day before handing the ball to multiple pitchers creates a difficult challenge.
Guardians vs. Rays Prediction on Winner for ALCS Game 6 – 10/19/26
Here are the key stats and trends behind our Guardians vs. Rays prediction on the winner for Monday's ALCS Game 6.
Unless otherwise noted, data used in this article is from FanGraphs, Baseball Savant, and MLB.com.
- I like Tampa Bay to close out this series at home, a place where they've had tremendous success. The Rays went 58-27-0 straight up at home this season; their 68.2% home win rate ranks second in baseball behind the Milwaukee Brewers.
- Postseason baseball comes down to pitching, and the Rays are in a much better position when it comes to that. Peralta's already shut down the Guardians once, while Cleveland will rely on a bunch of bullpen arms worked to the bone.
- Peralta has fared much better at home all season, pitching to the tune of a 3.77 FIP compared to a 4.86 mark away from home.
- The Rays' offense has also been better at home, owning a 108 wRC+ at the Trop compared to 100 wRC+ on the road.
- Cleveland's wRC+ drops from 100 at home to 94 in road outings.
- Tampa Bay also has a slight bullpen advantage, owning the best relief xFIP in the postseason (2.80).
Guardians vs. Rays Picks, Player Stats for ALCS on PrizePicks: 10/19/26
Here are two Guardians vs. Rays player picks to consider for Monday's ALCS Game 6. Today's MLB picks on PrizePicks include Chase DeLauter and Freddy Peralta.
Guardians RF/DH Chase DeLauter vs. Rays: 5.5 Hitter Fantasy Score
- DeLauter has recorded 11 postseason hits, matching a Cleveland franchise record for a single postseason.
- He doubled off Peralta in Game 2, showing that he can find a gap against the right-hander even when the Rays' starter is at his best.
- DeLauter owns an impressive 133 wRC+ in October and has done a phenomenal job of drawing walks (14.0%) and putting the ball in play (7.0% strikeout rate).
- “Fastball” Freddy Peralta surprises nobody with what pitch he throws the most. That’s good news for DeLauter, however, as he led all Guardians by a wide margin with a 1.56 wFB/C (fastball runs above average per 100 pitches) during the regular season.
{{mlb_offer_banner="/style-system/ui-components-playbook"}}
Rays P Freddy Peralta vs. Guardians: 4 Strikeouts
- Peralta has already demonstrated success in this spot, striking out 6 Guardians en route to a Rays Game 2 victory.
- He recorded 15 swings and misses in that outing, underscoring how effective his stuff was against Cleveland's hitters.
- Several Peralta heaters checked in at 99 mph or faster, showing the Rays' approach is working, as his velocity is higher than it's been in a few years.
- The Guardians have struggled to hit the fastball in October, ranking eighth among the 12 postseason teams with a wFB/C of -1.12.
- Peralta has had better strikeout stuff at home, owning an 8.87 K/9 compared to 7.68 on the road.
Make Guardians vs. Rays Picks on PrizePicks
The Rays are one win away from the World Series, and Peralta gives them an advantage on the mound. The Guardians will need a stronger offensive performance and an effective bullpen plan to keep their season alive.

item.title: [FanSided] Projecting MLB free agency deals for Tarik Skubal and baseball's biggest stars
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline

item.content:encoded:
MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point.
What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according to FanSided's Robert Murray) with projected contracts and destinations.
LHP Tarik Skubal
Projected deal: 9 years, $378 million ($42 million AAV) with New York Mets
Regardless of how CBA negotiations shake out, Tarik Skubal's long-rumored $400 million price tag may ultimately prove to be an overestimation. There's a reason no pitcher has ever received such a paycheck, Shohei Ohtani notwithstanding. Still, Skubal should become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history. His durability, both in-game and season-long, combined with razor-sharp stuff in the prime of his career, should give teams the confidence to invest in Skubal over an extended period.
The Dodgers are the natural landing spot after acquiring him at the trade deadline, but the Mets are baseball's richest team and there's mounting pressure for New York to start competing, in a serious way, with Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor. Skubal is the ultimate floor-raiser in a rotation, and he'd form a mean one-two punch with breakout ace Nolan McLean.
OF Seiya Suzuki
Projected deal: 4 years, $100 million ($25 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Seiya Suzuki is probably the best bat available in free agency. The 32-year-old outfielder has been a model of consistency for the Cubs, with at least 20 home runs and an .800-plus OPS in three straight seasons. He's a plus defender in right field, too, where he posted career-best metrics in 2026. Suzuki has a rocket-like arm and consistently holds runners from the back corner.
Plenty of teams will take an interest in Suzuki's right-handed power profile; he draws walks and operates with sage discipline in the batter's box, despite occasionally elevated strikeout numbers. In the end, Toronto represents the most logical intersection of need and financial firepower to outbid the field.
OF Randy Arozarena
Projected deal: 5 years, $110 million ($22 million AAV) with Philadelphia Phillies
Randy Arozarena set new career highs in average (.281), OPS (.865) and home runs (26) in his walk year, emerging as one of the few bright spots on an otherwise disappointing Mariners team. He's more adequate than exceptional with his glove, but Arozarena provides middle-order power and he's a great personality hire.
The Phillies need Arozarena's bat and competitive fire in equal measure, plus he can help to safely return Bryce Harper to first base next season. Philadelphia desperately needs a right-handed slugger behind Harper in the lineup; the ability to finally add some stability to the outfield depth chart, as opposed to a 2026 rewind of the Adolis García or Max Kepler situations, should greatly appeal to a desperate Dave Dombrowski.
3B Teruaki Sato
Projected deal: 3 years, $75 million ($25 million AAV) with New York Yankees
Teruaki Sato is the most accomplished international free agent hoping to come Stateside this offseason. An MVP candidate in Japan's NPB, Sato hit .306 this year with 39 home runs and a .991 OPS. There are swing-and-miss and defense concerns, not dissimilar to the vague uncertainties that tanked Munetaka Murakami's stock last winter. Murakami ended up on a two-year deal with the White Sox, which he immediately outperformed.
Sato's left-handed power and upside at 27 years old could mean his market flourishes. But, given the baked-in gambles that come with signing an international free agent, he could end up getting lowballed, much like Murakami. A three-year, $75 million contract gives Sato a nice payday upfront while still hedging against potential struggles with a short-term framework. The Yankees need an infield slugger and have the money to roll the dice, so to speak, on Sato's immense talent.
LHP Trevor Rogers
Projected deal: 3 years, $60 million ($20 million) with Baltimore Orioles
Trevor Rogers has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency over the years, but he's coming off of two strong campaigns in Baltimore — and he's only 28 years old, so there's room left to establish himself as more than a third or fourth starter type. He couldn't recapture the success of 2025, when Rogers returned from injury to post a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts, but his 4.03 ERA last season does not capture the strength of his stuff (3.60 xERA). Moreover, the career-high 30 starts and 169.2 innings pitched was a nice addition to his résumé.
Teams will probably balk at dropping a full bag on Rogers' doorstep, ultimately, which opens the door for a short-term contract (probably with an opt-out clause or two) and a return to Baltimore. The Orioles need pitching badly and there are precious few better options than Rogers floating around the open market. This contract could turn into a total bargain.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Projected deal: 4 years, $84 million ($21 million AAV) with Chicago Cubs
Freddy Peralta's walk year has been a roller coaster of emotions. He bombed in New York after the Mets dealt multiple top-100 prospects to acquire him in an offseason trade. Then, after relocating to Tampa at the trade deadline, Peralta started slow before gradually picking up steam in September. Down the stretch and into the playoffs, he has looked more like the Cy Young candidate we witnessed in Milwaukee last season.
Peralta has not made the strongest case to prospective suitors in 2026, so a one-year, high-AAV deal to "prove it" is on the table. Ultimately, however, the 30-year-old should still be able to coax a substantial multi-year offer out of a desperate contender. His longtime NL Central rivals, the Cubs, are one such desperate contender. Peralta could join with the now-healthy Cade Horton and Justin Steele to revitalize Chicago's World Series hopes for 2027.
C Ryan Jeffers
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Minnesota Twins
The catcher market is tough to project, as there are so few who can hit like Ryan Jeffers. He was excellent in Minnesota this season, with 14 home runs and an .814 OPS in roughly half a season. He's the best catcher on the market, but Jeffers is not exactly lauded for his defense nor his game management behind the plate. He is not without injury concerns either, while even the best catchers end up in a timeshare eventually (especially when, like Jeffers, their glovework can be problematic).
Since there is such an absence of reliable hitters at the catcher position, Jeffers should be able to land a solid multi-year deal in the middle of his prime. A return to the Twins should not be discounted, even with Eduardo Tait and Vahn Lackey coming up through the Minors on accelerated timelines. Minnesota made a conscious decision not to trade him at the deadline, after all. The Twins would probably like to compete next season.
RHP Michael King
Projected deal: five years, $120 million ($24 million AAV) with San Diego Padres
Michael King returned to San Diego last winter on a backloaded three-year deal with opt outs. After an excellent showing in the playoffs, he will probably axe the remaining two years and $66 million on that contract in hopes of securing more guaranteed money this winter. King is not the sexiest name on the pitching market by any stretch, but he has made himself into a dependable workhorse with October equity.
The Padres clearly love King and new ownership, with their stated intention to build a contender, will probably consent to a reworked contract. San Diego has a paper-thin rotation as is. Losing King without a viable alternative in place could be disastrous, as the Padres don't have the trade ammo to compensate for a free agency exodus.
2B Brandon Lowe
Projected deal: 3 years, $66 million ($22 million AAV) with Pittsburgh Pirates
Brandon Lowe arrived in Pittsburgh via offseason trade and immediately became the most bankable presence in their lineup, with 35 home runs, 96 RBI and an .824 OPS. The 32-year-old can get in trouble with swing-and-miss, but he's a slugging outlier at second base. Moreover, Lowe quietly posted some of the best defensive metrics in MLB last season after struggling for years on the defensive end. It's fair to be skeptical about Lowe's ability to sustain this elite defense into his mid-30s, but he did everything he could to maximize his value as a free agent.
To that point, it's hard to imagine the Pirates letting Lowe walk without a fight. Pittsburgh threw more money around last offseason, with the front office clearly committed to changing their postseason fortunes. It did not come together in 2026, but Pittsburgh has a dangerous lineup and a very talented pitching staff. There's potential for a breakthrough in 2027, especially if Lowe sticks around.
LHP Adrián Morejón
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Adrián Morejón's mystery-shrouded absence in San Diego's NLDS loss to Milwaukee was a tough pill to swallow, but once again, the Padres end the season feeling like the second-best team in the National League. They were able to at least put a scare into the Brewers where even the Dodgers could not. Part of the reason for San Diego's success this season, despite dramatic fluctuations from their lineup, was an elite bullpen. Morejón was only the setup man to Mason Miller, but the 27-year-old southpaw is still among the best relievers in baseball.
Over the past three seasons, Morejón has a 2.58 ERA with 248 strikeouts in 223.1 innings. It's hard to find a more steadfast high-leverage arm, especially one as young as Morejón. He could get some real length on his contract in a reliever-needy marketplace. The Blue Jays figure to be as aggressive as any team this offseason; Morejón setting up Louis Varland, with Tyler Rogers and Spencer Miles to cover other late-inning spots, is a tantalizing proposition.

item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week, White Sox GM Chris Getz spoke to the media for the first time since Chicago’s ALDS Game 5 loss against the Guardians. Getz reflected on the season and provided some updates on the future. Among the topics of conversation were positions the White Sox will pursue upgrades in during the upcoming offseason, with Getz emphasizing the starting rotation as an obvious area of need. I previously discussed a few starting pitching options I’d like to see the White Sox pursue, so this will be a bit of a different conversation. Let’s discuss a dream target, a realistic target, and a mistake the White Sox could make in their pitching search.
Dream Target: LHP Tarik Skubal
It’s impossible to discuss the pitching free agent class without mentioning two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the best pitcher available by a wide margin and one of the most dominant arms in all of baseball. The soon-to-be 30-year-old spent the first six and a half seasons with the Tigers before a midseason trade sent him to the Dodgers. He won the Cy Young Award in both 2024 and 2025, with a 2.39 and 2.21 ERA in each year, and would’ve been squarely in the mix for 2026 as well if not for an injury that cost him six weeks in May and June.
Do I think the White Sox have any chance at landing Tarik Skubal? Probably not. To be honest, I’d be surprised if they’re even interested. But Chicago has a very low payroll and an obvious need in the starting rotation. In theory, they could add Skubal for $30-40 million a year and still have payroll room for other upgrades on the roster. They’re a young, exciting team who seems to be just beginning their competitive window, so it’s a destination that could be appealing for Skubal. He’ll no doubt have his pick though, and it’s hard to see the White Sox competing financially with some of the other markets. I guess one can dream.
Realistic Target: RHP Tyler Mahle
Maybe big-game hunting isn’t realistic for the White Sox this offseason, but there’s no reason they can’t add at least one impact starting pitcher in free agency. Braves righty Tyler Mahle is an interesting veteran arm who shined during the second half of the season and into the playoffs. While most pitchers traded at the deadline struggled in their new home, Mahle posted a 1.99 ERA in nine starts with Atlanta and allowed just two earned runs in 13.1 innings in the Postseason. Mahle turned 32 in September and will be looking to leverage his strong finish into a solid contract. Perhaps a two or three-year deal could be in the cards for a player who’s always had a productive career but has battled frequent injuries. Mahle would be a strong veteran presence in the White Sox rotation and has a recent history of Postseason success. He could be one of the names on Chicago’s target list.
Mistake: LHP Robbie Ray
Left-hander Robbie Ray was one of the most talked about names ahead of the trade deadline, and the Giants ultimately dealt him within their division to the San Diego Padres. Some concerning metrics made Ray a prime candidate for regression, and he posted just a 5.02 ERA in nine starts for San Diego down the stretch. Still, he has back to back seasons with an ERA under 3.70, so he’s deserving of a big league deal this offseason. I don’t think that should be the White Sox, however. Ray is now 35 years old and his underlying metrics were scary in 2026. He pitched in two ballparks that heavily favor pitchers, whereas Chicago is a more hitter-friendly environment. Ray is a veteran who has struggled in the playoffs in his career, and his age is a real concern. I’d stay away here if I were the White Sox.

item.title: [fansided.com] The stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal, with one giant asterisk standing in their way
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. item.content:encoded:
The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing?
Well, here's a look at why the Mets make more sense for Skubal than you might think, and what might stand in their way of making this dream of arguably the best pitcher in the sport playing out the rest of his prime in Queens a reality.
The Dodgers' lack of aggression might play into the Mets' hands
When the Los Angeles Dodgers traded for Tarik Skubal, MLB fans not only assumed they'd automatically win a World Series title, but they also assumed that the Dodgers would easily extend Skubal, given their recent history of spending on star-level talent. It's absolutely possible that the Dodgers do choose to re-sign Skubal, but look at what ESPN's Alden Gonzalez had to say about that.
"Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will probably want to get something done with his client before the lockout, but it would be really difficult for the Dodgers to justify signing Skubal to a massive deal before knowing what MLB's economic model will look like," Gonzalez wrote. "If there is a cap-and-floor system in the next collective bargaining agreement, there will be some sort of phase-in period. But it will undoubtedly impact the Dodgers in the near future. It would be a major risk to sign Skubal before knowing what they're signing up for."
To sum up, Gonzalez is predicting that Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will likely want to get a deal done with his top client before the expected lockout at the beginning of December, but the Dodgers would want to wait until after the lockout so they know what the economic model of the sport will look like. This makes a ton of sense, given the massive amount of money they've already committed to 2027 and beyond. It's worth noting that this is just Gonzalez's belief, and not a sourced report.
If the Dodgers won't aggressively pursue Skubal before December 1, why can't the Mets be the team to give him an offer he can't refuse? It's not like the Mets haven't been in this position before.
The Mets have beaten the competition to the punch pre-lockout before
Just like a lockout is looming this offseason, one loomed back in the 2021 offseason, when Max Scherzer was a free agent. Scherzer, who was represented by Scott Boras, made it clear that he wanted to sign before the league locked the players out, and he did just that, coming to terms on a three-year, $130 milllion deal with, guess who, the New York Mets.
Now, say what you want about how the deal aged (Scherzer pitched brilliantly in 2022 but struggled in that year's postseason and was traded at the 2023 trade deadline), but the Mets beat the Dodgers and a couple of other teams to the punch to sign the future Hall of Famer on a deal that paid him well over $40 million annually.
Can't that history repeat itself? The Mets won the Scherzer sweepstakes not because they were some powerhouse, but because the Dodgers didn't want to go above and beyond to sign him as the Mets did. Reports suggest Skubal would like to sign pre-lockout and the Dodgers don't want to go above and beyond. Why can't the Mets do what they've already done and give their fan base something to get excited about before the lockout?
If the Dodgers and Mets won't pay Tarik Skubal, what team will?
Let's just assume that both the Dodgers and the Mets decide that paying Skubal is not in their best interest. Is there another team out there willing to spend the $300-to-$400 million on Skubal that he'll likely be asking for?
The New York Yankees are often willing spenders, but with a ton of money invested in starting pitchers like Gerrit Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodon, would they pay Skubal before addressing their offense? The Philadelphia Phillies should be eager to spend after another early elimination, but again, is paying on pitching in their best interest? The Chicago Cubs could certainly use the pitching, but they've never even handed out a $200 million contract. Would they give $300+ million to Skubal? The Toronto Blue Jays have the money and the need for pitching help, but they also just paid Dylan Cease handsomely last winter and finished last in runs scored this past season. A return to the Detroit Tigers would be awesome, but that feels unrealistic.
There're other teams like the San Francisco Giants and the Los Angeles Angels who might show interest, but again, there isn't really a perfect fit. If the Mets and Dodgers won't meet an outlandish asking price, which team will?
The Mets have a clear need for a high-end starting pitcher
The Mets are building a strong rotation, with youngsters like Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton in the fold, but the team lacks a true ace. They hoped Freddy Peralta would fill that void when they acquired him from the Brewers in the 2025 offseason, but that experiment flopped spectacularly.
It's hard to see Skubal flopping, though, at least in 2027. He remains one of, if not the best pitcher in the sport, and even after an early-season injury scare, Skubal ended his season with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts. He's as dynamic as they come, and would instantly make the Mets true postseason contenders.
If they don't sign Skubal, who else could they realistically get? The next-best options, such as Michael King, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, aren't exactly aces. They could potentially swing a trade, but doing so is easier said than done. It feels like Skubal or bust when it comes to getting a bona fide ace.
Would David Stearns be willing to abandon his starting pitching philosophy to sign Tarik Skubal?
We know that the Mets have the need, the money and the location necessary to lure Skubal to the team, but would the individual responsible for making such a move, David Stearns, be willing to do so? Stearns has famously been averse to handing massive deals to starting pitchers, passing on guys like Corbin Burnes, Max Fried and Dylan Cease, to name a few, and instead relying on shorter-term gambles.
Most of these have not paid off, which is partially why the Mets have missed the playoffs in back-to-back years, but will there be a mindset shift? Will Stearns suddenly go from a guy unwilling to offer more than three years to a pitcher over the age of 30 to willing to meet Skubal's demands?
That's an answer we're soon going to learn the answer to, and it could be the difference in Skubal joining the Mets or signing elsewhere. If Stearns is all in, the stars feel like they're aligning for something special to happen.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Phillies Boss Pinpoints ‘Really, Really Good’ Infield Replacement After Trea Turner Decision
item.dc:creator: Peter Chawaga; Contributor
item.description: The Philadelphia Phillies head into yet another offseason with questions to answer about their roster construction after an early postseason exit. Earlier this week, during his end of season press conference, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski made it clear that the team needs to improve defensively, and one of its biggest decisions could involve a veteran who remains central to the franchise. "From a defensive perspective, we are very clear," Dombrowski said of Trea Turner, accord
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies head into yet another offseason with questions to answer about their roster construction after an early postseason exit.
Earlier this week, during his end of season press conference, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski made it clear that the team needs to improve defensively, and one of its biggest decisions could involve a veteran who remains central to the franchise.
"From a defensive perspective, we are very clear," Dombrowski said of Trea Turner, according to the New York Post's Matt Ehalt. "He knows he has to be better at shortstop. And I told him that it's really mandatory that he's like that."
Though Dombrowski made it clear that Turner no longer has a lock on the shortstop position, the Phillies seem reliant on the long-term contracts already on the books, including his. But during the same press conference, the front office boss singled out one new player who could join the roster next season.
Philadelphia Phillies Boss Highlights Trea Turner Replacement After Harsh Warning
If Turner cannot return to his previous defensive form, Dombrowski made it clear that he will consider other options. Initially, it seems most likely that the team would shift Turner to second base or to the outfield and move Bryson Stott to shortstop.
But the Phillies president also pinpointed an exciting young infielder as an example of a new player who could join the mix next season.
"I'm not going to put it on his back, but we think a guy like Aidan Miller is a really, really good player," Dombrowski said, according to MLB.com's Todd Zolecki. "You see all the young players that have jumped into playing this year and the years that they had. Aidan Miller, when he's healthy, he's as good as any of them."
Turner is entering the fourth season of his 11-year, $300 million contract, and the Phillies have not ruled out keeping him at shortstop. But Dombrowski singled out Miller as an intriguing option to take some pressure off of the team's veteran core of position players, and it seems that if and when he does receive a promotion, he could be taking over the shortstop role.
Philadelphia Phillies' Trea Turner Replacement Could Already Be In The Organization
Miller's potential makes him an interesting name to watch as the Phillies consider their infield options, although his arrival should not be viewed as a certainty for Opening Day.
The prospect entered 2026 as Philadelphia's top-ranked position prospect but lost much of the season to a back injury that required surgery in June. He returned to action in September, appearing in four regular-season games across the Florida Complex League and Double-A Reading before helping Reading during its Eastern League championship run.
For now, Turner has an opportunity to retain his position by improving defensively. But with Dombrowski publicly identifying Miller as a potential contributor, the Phillies have another avenue to explore if their veteran shortstop cannot deliver the necessary improvement.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies have locked in their manager after removing the interim tag from Don Mattingly. Who their regular shortstop will be during season is a question that Trea Turner will have to answer.
The 33-year-old Turner was challenged this week by Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski to improve his defense, otherwise Turner will be taking on a new position within the team.
"From a defensive perspective we were very clear," Dombrowski said of his conversation with Turner. "He knows he has to be better at shortstop. And I told him that it's really mandatory that he's like that. He feels he can play, and if he plays shortstop like he did in '25, he can play shortstop. But if he plays it like he did in '26, he can't. And he totally understands that."
Turner committed 21 errors during the 2026 season, the second-highest season total of his 12-year MLB career. His highest amount came in 2023, his first season with the Phillies. According to MLB, his -10 Outs Above Average this past season was 39th out of 42 qualified shortstops. That is a vast drop off from his +17 OAA in 2025, which was third-best.
Defensive issues were a season-long storyline for Turner, who played 154 games at shortstop. While Mattingly spoke with several other players, including Bryce Harper, about changing positions, no conversations were held with Turner.
The Phillies have options if the time comes where Turner needs a position change. Bryson Stott played shortstop before Turner joined in Dec. 2022. Prospects Aidan Miller and Bryan Rincon could end up there later on in the 2027 season. There is also free agency if Dombrowski wants to find cover before Spring Training — barring a lockout, of course.
There are seven years and $190 million remaining on Turner's contract, which includes a no-trade clause.
"I can't control the daily banter about what takes place," Dombrowski said. "He's not the first player I've ever been around that was surrounded by that. He's a smart guy. He knows he needs to get better, and I think he'll deal with it. But he's got a long time to be here."

item.title: [MLB.com] LIVE: Brewers-Dodgers NLCS Game 4 (FS1/FOX One)
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen; Adam McCalvy; AJ Cassavell
item.description: Milwaukee brings a commanding 3-0 lead into Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. But the Dodgers are the champs until they’re not, and they’ve faced plenty of adversity on their way to World Series titles in each of the past two seasons. Never like this though. In all best-of-seven postseason series, teams with a 3-0 lead have gone on to win that series 41 times out of 42 -- with 32 of those series ending as sweeps. item.content:encoded:
Milwaukee brings a commanding 3-0 lead into Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. But the Dodgers are the champs until they’re not, and they’ve faced plenty of adversity on their way to World Series titles in each of the past two seasons.
Never like this though. In all best-of-seven postseason series, teams with a 3-0 lead have gone on to win that series 41 times out of 42 -- with 32 of those series ending as sweeps. Only two teams have ever even forced a Game 7 after trailing 3-0, and only the 2004 Red Sox, in the ALCS against the Yankees, have come all the way back to win.
“It's certainly possible,” said Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, himself a fabled part of that Red Sox rally. “I've lived it. And I think the thing is that our guys have been battle-tested. … It's an elimination game. We've played in a lot of elimination games. We've just got to get a win.”
While the Dodgers chase baseball history, the Brewers can make a bit of their own with a win on Thursday. A year ago, they were swept by the Dodgers in the very same round. If they can return the favor, they would become the first team to be swept out of the playoffs, only to sweep the same team -- in any postseason series -- a year later. But they’re not getting ahead of themselves.
“We have yet to complete anything,” Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio said through an interpreter. “The job's not finished for us. So we have to come with the same mentality. Which is to win.”
Here’s what you need to know about Game 4:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 4 is currently airing nationally on FS1.
All series are available in the US on MLB.TV with authentication to a participating Pay TV provider. Games also are available live internationally, although not in Canada. Sportsnet is MLB's exclusive English language broadcaster in Canada for every Postseason game, while TVA Sports will be covering the entire AL Postseason and the World Series in French and Broadcaster RDS will cover the entire NL Postseason in French.
The Brewers picked Drohan from among a plethora of fresh options to start what amounts to a bullpen game. Left-handers Kyle Harrison and Drohan and right-hander Chad Patrick have been on the roster for both the NLDS and NLCS, but have yet to pitch in any of the Brewers’ first seven games. Midseason pickup Dustin May, the former Dodger who won a World Series ring with L.A. in 2020, pitched an inning in NLCS Game 2 on what would have been a bullpen day had he been lined up to start Thursday. They are all options to come in behind Drohan, who had a 4.19 ERA in 33 games/19 starts and shifted to the bullpen late in the season when he came upon a loose innings limit. He thrived in short stints, posting a 1.47 ERA as a reliever. It will be his career postseason debut.
The Dodgers' 7-0 postseason record when Glasnow pitches is more of a quirk than anything else, but the right-hander has gotten the results to back it up. In four starts and three relief appearances, Glasnow has recorded a 1.73 ERA (five earned runs in 26 innings). Glasnow had command issues when he last pitched against the Braves in NLDS Game 4 -- issuing five walks -- but limited the damage to one run in 4 2/3 innings.
What are the starting lineups?
Brewers: The lineup the Brewers used against right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 produced the second postseason game in franchise history in which five different players tallied multiple hits. Against Glasnow in Game 4, they hope for a similar result with the same group.
Dodgers: Not only are the Dodgers sticking with Shohei Ohtani despite his lingering right biceps and left knee issues, they're bumping him up to leadoff for a must-win game. He and a scuffling Will Smith -- batting cleanup for Game 4 -- were dropped in the lineup in the past couple games, but the fact that both contributed to L.A.'s lone run-scoring rally in Game 3 likely played a role in Roberts' decision to elevate them Thursday.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Brewers: Right-handed setup man Abner Uribe, who has appeared in each of the first seven games of the postseason, finally wilted a bit in Game 3, walking three batters ahead of Smith’s two-run double in the sixth inning. But left-hander DL Hall kept the game on track by stopping the rally there and recording seven enormous outs. Then Trevor Megill logged a four-out save. That’s a lot of work for those last two arms, so lefty Aaron Ashby figures to play a prominent role in Game 4 if the score is tight.
Dodgers: It's all hands on deck, with the possible exception of Justin Wrobleski, who threw 32 pitches to cover the final 1 2/3 innings of Game 3. Roberts made a point of saying that he will get closer Edwin Díaz --- the only Dodgers reliever who has not pitched this series -- into Game 4.
Any injuries of note?
Brewers: None.
Dodgers: Ohtani (right biceps, left knee) and Freeman (right knee) are managing lingering injuries. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option. Blake Treinen (right shoulder inflammation) is unlikely to pitch this postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Brewers: Chourio’s .642 OPS in this postseason doesn’t tell anything about his impact. His leadoff home run in Game 3 marked his second homer of the 2026 postseason and sixth of his career, breaking a brief tie with William Contreras for the most homers in Brewers’ postseason history. Three of them have led off a postseason game, which matched Hall of Famer Derek Jeter, Jimmy Rollins and Ohtani for the second-most in history, trailing only Kyle Schwarber, who has five leadoff home runs in the postseason. And with his 18th career postseason RBI, Chourio also broke a tie with Hall of Famer Andruw Jones for the most postseason RBIs prior to a player’s 23rd birthday. … With his eighth-inning base hit, Contreras became the first Brewers player with 10 hits in this postseason.
Dodgers: Tucker (.304) has consistently swung the bat well through seven games, but he has been the exception to the rule for a cold Dodgers offense. In Game 3, Ohtani (113.5 mph single) and Smith (two-run double) showed some positive signs, but they have been L.A.'s most notable slumping bats this postseason.
Anything else fans might want to know?
•  Orel Hershiser and Mike Scioscia will throw out the ceremonial first pitch and say, "It's time for Dodger baseball!" as part of the pregame ceremonies.
• According to the Elias Sports Bureau, this is the eighth time two teams met in the postseason one year after one swept the other in the previous postseason. The only team to be swept and then win a rematch the following postseason is the 1923 Yankees, who won that year's World Series over the New York Giants in six games.
• Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said it struck him that it’s been 44 years since the Brewers made it to the World Series, and 44 is one of the franchise’s retired numbers for Hall of Famer Hank Aaron. This year marked the 50th anniversary of Aaron’s 755th and final home run, which he hit while playing for the Brewers in 1976.
• This marks the sixth time a team has taken a 3-0 series lead against the reigning World Series champion in a best-of-seven series. Four of the previous five -- 1990 WS, Reds vs A’s; 1966 WS, Orioles vs Dodgers; 1963 WS, Dodgers vs Yankees; 1914 WS, Boston Braves vs Philadelphia Athletics -- ended in a sweep. The other (2017 NLCS, Dodgers vs Cubs) concluded with the Dodgers winning in five games.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Guardians ALCS Game 3 FAQ, lineups (1 ET, TBS/HBO Max)
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Keegan Matheson; Adam Berry
item.description: CLEVELAND -- It’s a new day in the ALCS, as the Rays and Guardians have shifted their matchup back to Cleveland tied up at 1-1. The Rays' 3-1 win in Game 2 shifted this series back into focus after the Guardians pulled off a 7-3 come-from-behind win in the opener. item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- It’s a new day in the ALCS, as the Rays and Guardians have shifted their matchup back to Cleveland tied up at 1-1.
The Rays' 3-1 win in Game 2 shifted this series back into focus after the Guardians pulled off a 7-3 come-from-behind win in the opener. We’ve seen each team’s best, and as these pitching staffs get stretched even thinner as the series wears on, they’ll need to lean on the identities they’ve built in 2026.
“It’s going to be a challenging place to play,” said Rays manager Kevin Cash. “We played there not too long ago in the postseason. That's as good an atmosphere as you're going to see. They've got a great fan base that's going to be behind their team. I'd like to think we can carry our momentum into there and just play good baseball for Game 3.”
Step back a few feet for a wider view, and this Guardians team has still won four of its past five games. The club ran into a Game 2 buzzsaw named Freddy Peralta, whose fastball was nearly unhittable, but Cleveland is still in an excellent spot after stealing Game 1.
“We feel great. Obviously we would have loved to have taken [Game 2],” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “That would have been really big. And we had our position and our opportunities to do that. But going home 1-1, to go have three games in front of our fans in Cleveland, we feel really good about that. And we're excited to get it going.”
The pitching matchup has the potential to lean in the Guardians’ favor, too, with Gavin Williams starting on regular rest, fresh off a dominant outing against the White Sox to clinch the ALDS. For the Rays, Griffin Jax has been officially named the starter, and while he spent the majority of the season working in a true starter’s role, he pitched two innings of relief against the Yankees in Game 3 of the ALDS, throwing just 32 pitches.
This series is still waiting for its first show-stopping moment, too, with all eyes on José Ramírez for the Guardians and Junior Caminero for the Rays. Ramírez's series has been up-and-down so far, from a solid Game 1 to a crucial error that opened the door in Game 2, while Caminero is still searching for his first career postseason home run.
There’s history on the line here, too, for whichever team advances to represent the American League in the World Series. The Rays haven’t won the World Series since entering the league in 1998 and have only reached the big stage twice (2008, 2020). The Guardians, on the other hand, still carry the weight of the longest World Series drought in the big leagues at 77 seasons, stretching all the way back to 1948.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Rays-Guardians American League Championship Series is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET on Thursday at Progressive Field. Due to inclement weather in the forecast, the original start time of 6 p.m. was moved up. The game will be broadcast on TBS and HBO Max. 
Spanish-language game broadcasts will be available on UniMas for the ALCS, and Spanish-language radio broadcasts will be available on Univision’s TUDN Radio.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Griffin Jax, RHP
Key Stats: 0.90 ERA over his past five appearances
Nick Martinez started ALDS Game 3 for the Rays, but they will turn to Jax this time after using him as a reliever against the Yankees, with Martinez likely in line to pitch Game 4 on Friday. Jax has been excellent since a rough return from the injured list on Sept. 2 after a bout of right elbow discomfort, permitting only two runs on 10 hits and four walks while striking out 19 in 20 innings over his last four regular-season starts and his Game 3 relief outing at Yankee Stadium. Jax is presumably prepared for Cleveland’s inclement weather, having pitched for Minnesota for most of his career, and he’s put up impressive numbers (including a 2.19 ERA, 0.89 WHIP and 20 strikeouts) in 13 relief appearances at Progressive Field.
Guardians: Gavin Williams, RHP
Key Stats: 1.54 ERA, 24 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings in ALDS
The Guardians officially named Williams their Game 3 starter on Wednesday afternoon, setting the 27-year-old up for a start on normal rest following his heroic performance in the ALDS, when he made two starts and an emergency relief appearance against the White Sox. After he recorded the final three outs of Game 4, Williams came back on one day’s rest in Game 5 and tied a franchise postseason record in strikeouts (12) to help Cleveland beat Chicago, 2-0, to advance. Williams starting Game 3 also positions him to start a potential Game 7 of this series on Tuesday, on normal rest.
What are the starting lineups?
Rays: With Williams on the mound, the Rays are going with their standard lineup against right-handers, with the “Big Three” followed by their other left-handed hitters. They're staying with Jonny DeLuca, who’s started every postseason game so far, over Cedric Mullins in center field.
Guardians: Patrick Bailey is back behind the plate in Game 3. He and Williams have been a customary battery this season, and Bailey is swinging a hot bat this postseason. The Guards are sticking with the standard lineup they’ve had in this series.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Guardians: Vogt will have a full bullpen at his disposal after the off-day, and will work getting the ball to closer Cade Smith. He and Hunter Gaddis did not appear in Game 2, after both pitched in each of the Guardians’ first six contests this postseason. Setup man Erik Sabrowski also did not pitch in Game 2 and will be working off two days’ rest.
Rays: The Rays should be in good shape after Wednesday’s off-day, although this will be the first time since the regular season that they’ve played three consecutive days in a row. Left-hander Ian Seymour has clearly established himself as a top setup option in front of closer Bryan Baker, and lefty Cam Booser has also been tasked with getting big outs against left-handed hitters. Right-hander Kevin Kelly and Tyler Wells are also setup options in front of Baker, who has recorded the save in each of Tampa Bay’s four wins this postseason.
Any injuries of note?
Guardians: None.
Rays: Caminero and DeLuca said they were fine after a nasty collision while chasing a foul ball in Game 1. Left-hander Shane McClanahan, who finished the regular season on the injured list due to left forearm tightness, was shut down for the rest of the postseason, Cash said on Sunday. Otherwise, nothing new.
Who is hot and who is not?
Guardians: Shawn Armstrong has allowed just one hit and struck out five batters in 5 1/3 scoreless innings over four postseason appearances. It’s been an impressive comeback after he missed two months with a left calf strain, before returning the final week of the regular season. DeLauter is hitting .346 (9-for-26) with just one strikeout in seven postseason games.
Rocchio is hitting .091 (2-for-22) in seven games.
Rays: Pretty much everyone who touched the mound for Tampa Bay in the ALDS and Game 2 of this series performed well, which is certainly promising for the team moving forward, even after some shaky bullpen work in Game 1. The Rays are starting to find some rhythm at the plate, too, with Caminero leading the way despite not yet having the big moment everyone’s expecting. Hicks drove in a couple runs in Game 2, and DeLuca had his second straight multihit game. Díaz is just 5-for-21 in the playoffs, and Mesa is only 3-for-18.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• Cleveland Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell will throw the ceremonial first pitch before Game 3.
• With his fifth-inning single in Game 2, Ramírez moved into second place in franchise history in postseason hits (49), breaking a tie with Kenny Lofton. Omar Vizquel (57) ranks first.
• Game 2 of the ALCS was Díaz’s 30th postseason game with the Rays, matching Evan Longoria for the most in franchise history. Game 3 should give Tampa Bay’s DH the club record.
• The Rays are 89-0 this year, including the regular season and postseason, when leading after eight innings. The last team to go a full year with a 1.000 winning percentage and at least 89 wins when leading after eight innings? The 2022 Mets, who went 90-0. The last team to do so in the AL was the 2002 Athletics (93-0).

item.title: [CBS Sports] The state of the second base position ahead of 2027: Fernando Tatis Jr. leads a thin Fantasy field
item.dc:creator: Chris Towers
item.description: The second base position is in rougher shape than I initially thought. There is useful depth available here for 2027, but it is light on real difference makers. And that is largely because of who isn't going to be eligible at second base. C.J. item.content:encoded:
The second base position is in rougher shape than I initially thought. There is useful depth available here for 2027, but it is light on real difference makers. And that is largely because of who isn't going to be eligible at second base.
C.J. Abrams won't be, at least to start, though he does seem very likely as of now to end up eligible at second base pretty early on in the season. That is, unfortunately, less true for the likes of Sal Stewart and Otto Lopez, two of the biggest breakout stars at the position, though for opposite reasons; Stewart because he just isn't good enough defensively to justify much time there, Lopez because he's probably too good at shortstop to move back to the keystone. You have something similar with Luis Garcia Jr. (likely just a first baseman moving forward) and Ceddanne Rafaela (too good in center field to play him anywhere else).
And they aren't the only ones losing eligibility for 2027. Curtis Mead, Casey Schmitt, Brooks Lee, Royce Lewis, and Zack Gelof were all at least useful starters at second base in 2026, and none of them played there enough to retain eligibility. Gelof's is the most frustrating case, because he played his 19th game at second base in late August and never appeared there again, coming just one appearance short of retaining eligibility. Even if you're skeptical of his 2026 breakout (as I am), losing him hurts the position.
Right now, I'd say there are maybe six second basemen I feel very good about as my starter for 2026, and then another few who seem like decent starters, and then a whole bunch of useful, but ultimately replaceable options. Does that mean second base is where we should play the positional scarcity game?
Well, if you are the type of Fantasy player who cares about such things, go for it. Second base looks like clearly the weakest position in Fantasy (non-catcher, anyway) for 2027, both in terms of impact bats and viable starting options. So, if you want to nudge Fernando Tatis up a few spots in your overall rankings to ensure you get elite production out of that lineup spot, go for it.
I don't really care all that much about positional scarcity, so I won't be doing much waiting there. I don't mind targeting Tatis in the first round, obviously, but the fact that he is second base eligible only plays a small factor. In part, that's because I just don't care that much about positional scarcity in drafts – we aren't as good as we think we are at projecting which positions will actually be weak and which will be strong in any given season, so I'll just try to draft the best players and not worry too much about which position they'll slot in at.
But I also don't care too much about positional scarcity at second base because plenty of guys unexpectedly gain eligibility there all of the time. Of all infield positions, it is the one where teams seem most willing to just toss a guy out there and see if they can handle it. Don't have enough range for shortstop or enough arm for third base? Get ready to learn second base, buddy.
Which is to say, second base is never actually as bad as it looks. Some hotshot shortstop prospect will probably find himself starting at second base on Opening Day that we can't see coming right now, or some veteran will find himself pushed there based on how his team's offseason goes. It happens every year, and while you probably shouldn't plan your draft around being able to plug someone in at second base unexpectedly, you surely will end up with more options than you expect once the games start. That's just the nature of the position.
For more on the state of the second base position, .
2026 Second Base Review
- Fernando Tatis Jr., SDP: .289 - 96 - 25 - 83 - 38
- Brice Turang, MIL: .268 - 102 - 21 - 100 - 19
- Brandon Lowe, PIT: .260 - 94 - 35 - 96 - 2
- Otto Lopez, MIA: .305 - 94 - 11 - 71 - 34
- Luis García Jr., NYY: .277 - 69 - 30 - 92 - 5
- Ceddanne Rafaela, BOS: .285 - 67 - 16 - 70 - 17
- Kody Clemens, MIN: .239 - 74 - 27 - 81 - 10
- Jazz Chisholm Jr., NYY: .231 - 69 - 19 - 55 - 41
- Luke Keaschall, MIN: .282 - 86 - 10 - 52 - 20
- Luis Arraez, PHI: .310 - 67 - 6 - 64 - 10
- Bryson Stott, PHI: .256 - 71 - 10 - 67 - 27
- Zack Gelof, ATH: .256 - 76 - 22 - 55 - 16
If we remove the players who won't be second base eligible in 2027, Ketel Marte, Ozzie Albies, Ezequiel Duran, and Nick Gonzales slide into the top 12. Which kind of highlights the point about the position: There were plenty of useful options, but few true difference makers. The replacement level at second base tends to be pretty high. However, the difference between, say, the 10th-best option at the position in 2026 and the 20th was a little under $3 in value in the FanGraphs Player Rater – at shortstop, the difference between No. 10 and No. 20 was closer to $5, for example.
Biggest Breakout from 2026
Otto Lopez, Marlins
Lopez slowed down considerably in the second half of the season but still had the breakout many suspected was lurking. He won't hit .305 ever again, but something like a .280 average, double-digit homers, and 25-plus steals is still valuable from a second baseman. Unfortunately, he won't open next season with second-base eligibility. Unless he gets traded to a team with a very good shortstop, he isn't likely to add it anytime soon. So we'll pivot to …
Kody Clemens, Twins
I guess? Clemens finished as the No. 7 second baseman thanks to a huge power breakout that saw him hit 27 homers. The counting stats beyond that were pretty iffy because he didn't really play against lefties earlier in the season. His .233/.286/.393 line against lefties isn't a disaster, but coming from a 30-year-old with clear defensive limitations, the Twins wouldn't be out of line to spend the offseason at least looking for a platoon partner for him. I think there's a pretty good chance we just saw the best season of Clemens' career. I wouldn't be looking to draft him as a starter in 2027 at this point, but if it looks like he's primed for an everyday role, you could definitely get a Brandon Lowe-esque outcome from him in a best-case scenario.
Biggest Bust from 2026
Yeah, I think we might be done here. There were some signs of life from Altuve immediately after the All-Star break, as he hit .308/.373/.440 in August, but he collapsed back to a sub-.700 OPS in September and hasn't posted an OPS north of .800 in a month since July of 2025. He doesn't really steal bases anymore and the Astros lineup is underwhelming enough that you really don't get much of a boost there. Even at a relatively weak position like second base, it just doesn't look like there's much reason to even draft Altuve in 2027, sadly.
Biggest rankings movers from 2026 to 2027
Up: Brandon Lowe, Free Agent; JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals; Kody Clemens, Twins
I understand why Lowe's price was as low as it was entering 2025, with a long list of injuries that had held him to less than 110 games in three straight seasons. But he played 134 games in 2025 and hit 31 homers, and the Fantasy community responded by only moving him up to around 175th in ADP. And of course, he went out and had an even better season in 2026, so surely his price will rise, right? We'll see where he lands in free agency. Lowe proved he can still be an everyday player and still make a significant impact, and there are few players at any position who give you as big an edge on the competition as Lowe does with homers at second base; Clemens is the only other player eligible at the position for 2027 who had more than 25 homers last season.
Wetherholt's rookie season was mostly a success. A second-half wrist injury saw his production collapse in August and September when he was healthy enough to play, but he was hitting .259/.356/.399 with a 23-homer, 16-steal pace at the All-Star break and he did it as a 23-year-old. I'm not sure there are too many superstar-level outcomes for Wetherholt – that wasn't really projected for him as a prospect, either – but there's enough pop in his bat to project some 25-homer outcomes here, and he could emerge as a 20-steal guy hitting at the top of the lineup, too. The .242 final batting average is a red flag, but with his contact skills, it's not unreasonable to expect something closer to the .275 range as he grows. It's a sneaky-exciting skill set for a guy who might get lost in the shuffle a bit among other, more obviously exciting young bats.
Down: Ketel Marte, Diamondbacks; Nico Hoerner, Cubs; Jose Altuve, Astros; Matt McLain, Reds
Marte's outlook for 2027 is at least somewhat in flux because he seems pretty likely to get traded away after all of the ... weirdness in Arizona. He took a step back in 2026, with his .249/.316/432 line clearly his worst since 2022. The underlying numbers were still plenty strong, if not quite as good as his previous few seasons. That's not unusual for a 32-year-old, and betting on a player multiple years into his 30s to bounce back after a down season is often a surefire way to invite disappointment. But if you go into next season expecting something like a .275 average and 25-plus homers (plus whatever run production his likely new home ballpark and lineup will allow), he should be a fine pick after the first four or so rounds are done.
Hoerner dipping down to just 23 steals in his age-29 season seems like a pretty bad sign. It doesn't mean he can't bounce back, but speed generally fades as a player hits their 30s, and the fact that it was combined with the lowest BABIP Hoerner has posted in any MLB season feels like an especially worrying sign. I don't mind betting on a bounceback when Hoerner will likely come very cheap, but if he isn't hitting near the top of the Cubs lineup, he might just be a Fantasy also-ran even if there is some positive regression; he scored just 62 runs in 2026!
There was some real hype around McLain after a massive Spring Training, which should serve as a reminder that, even with all of the information at our fingertips, your bias should still strongly tilt in the direction of dismissing Spring Training production. McLain still has a mildly intriguing power/speed combination, but after watching him flirt with the Mendoza Line in consecutive seasons, it's clear he just doesn't do enough well to make the 15 or so homers and 20 or so steals worth it.
Offseason preview
Who needs an upgrade most?
One thing to note with the Nationals specifically: They talked about moving C.J. Abrams to second base and played him there a handful of times in the second half of the 2026 season, so that might be a hole they fill internally. Shortstop would likely be filled by Nasim Nunez at first, with Seaver King as a candidate to win the job out of Spring Training and Eli Willits as the likely longer-term option.
Top impending free agents
- Jazz Chisholm
- Brandon Lowe
- Luis Arraez
- Gleyber Torres
A year ago, Chisholm looked like he might be a $200 million man when he hit free agency; now, it feels like a real question whether the Yankees will even extend a qualifying offer to him. He seems extremely likely to end up on the market for a long time before settling for the kind of one-year-plus-an-option contract that has become so common in recent years. He still has a very Fantasy-friendly skill set – 19 homers and 41 steals even in a down season! – but the batting average is actively harmful and the strikeouts really hurt his value in points leagues. I actually like the idea of betting on a bounceback in 2027, but Chisholm's poor contact skills will likely always leave him with a very low floor to worry about.
Trade candidates
- Ketel Marte, Diamondbacks
- Otto Lopez, Marlins
- Ozzie Albies, Braves
- Bryson Stott, Phillies
- Brendan Donovan, Mariners
Albies is a very interesting one, because his contract is still dirt cheap (just $7 million in 2027), but it's not clear he's even worth much more than that at this point. He hasn't been worth more than 1.4 WAR in a season since 2023; he is just 26th in WAR among second basemen since the start of 2025. Entering his age-30 season, is there really much reason to bet on a bounceback? He's cheap enough that the Braves will probably just keep him around, but he also probably isn't good enough for a team that truly aims to contend to keep starting every day, especially with how little they've gotten from the shortstop spot over the past few seasons.
Top 2027 rookies to know
- Michael Arroyo, Mariners
- Demetrio Crisantes, Diamondbacks
- Devin Fitz-Gerald, Nationals
- Max Anderson, tigers
The thing we have to remember is that shortstops end up being overrepresented in prospect rankings, while second- and third-basemen are inherently underrepresented. Shortstop prospects inevitably end up moving off the position at much higher rates than at any other position, so at least some of the big, flashy names at shortstop will move to second base. And that's good news, because the list of top prospects at second base heading into 2026 is pretty underwhelming! But we could see more interesting names like Franklin Arias, Seaver King, Luis Pena, or Leo De Vries end up playing enough second base to qualify there some time in 2027.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Early 2027 Fantasy Baseball Rankings: Top 20 at third base reveals how risky the position has become
item.dc:creator: Scott White
item.description: My expectation going into this exercise was that third base would be terrible, clearly the worst position for Fantasy in 2027. Now, I'm not sure. item.content:encoded:
My expectation going into this exercise was that third base would be terrible, clearly the worst position for Fantasy in 2027. Now, I'm not sure.
It's bad, yes, offering only six players that I'd feel great about drafting, but having just ranked second base a few days ago ... I don't know. Third base might be better.
- Early rankings: | | | 3B | SS | OF | SP | RP
Just look at the crossover players. Bryson Stott ranked 11th for me at second base. He's 16th here. Javier Sanoja, Willi Castro and Ezequiel Duran all placed in my top 20 at second base. None of them do here.
Second base may have safer options, by and large, but there's more upside to be found at third base. And while second base is losing a whole host of players due to eligibility restrictions, only one of real significance, Jazz Chisholm, is dropping out at third.
Note that the focus here is standard 5x5 scoring (such as Rotisserie leagues), but scroll a little further, and you'll see my rankings for points leagues as well.
| 1 | |
| Whatever doubts existed for Caminero heading into 2026 were thoroughly expunged by a second consecutive 40-homer campaign in which he nearly doubled his walk rate -- a telltale sign that he's now among the most feared hitters in the game. At 23, he's poised for a lengthy reign atop this position. | |
| 2 | |
| Between the massive increase in average bat speed and the pull-air rate verging on 30 percent, there's little reason to doubt Vargas' power contributions, and he's fast enough to continue impacting the stolen base category as well. Some will be inclined toward skepticism given the enormity of his breakthrough, but third base unfortunately doesn't allow for such nitpicking. | |
| 3 | |
| Stewart's totals were more impressive than his percentages in 2026, which could make him a polarizing player heading into the new season, but based on his minor league numbers, I think he has more ground to gain in strikeouts and pull-air rate. The 15 steals are the most iffy part of his 2026 stat line, judging by his 27th percentile sprint speed. | |
| 4 | |
| Ramirez's power completely vanished in the second half, when he hit just two home runs, which is concerning enough to dethrone him at the position he has long dominated. He does have a valid excuse for it, seeing as he was coming off a broken hamate bone during that time, and I'll note that his contact skills and base-stealing remained perfectly intact. Still, he doesn't get the full benefit of the doubt at age 34. | |
| 5 | |
| After a sluggish opening act in Chicago that positioned him to be a free agent bust, Bregman made some mechanical changes midseason that led to the sort of power production we hadn't seen from him since his 41-homer 2019. While the .317 batting average, 17 homers and 1.103 OPS that he delivered over his final 43 games isn't projectable over a full season, it makes him out to be a trustworthy choice at this thin position. | |
| 6 | |
| McGonigle had a historic rookie season in many ways, but not necessarily the most Fantasy-friendly ways, owing much to his superlative defense and on-base skills. How much power he can pack onto his 5-foot-9 frame, particularly at a restrictive venue, will go a long way toward determining his ceiling. Still, he has ground to gain in batting average and stolen bases. | |
| 7 | |
| The decline for Machado in 2026, while marked, was mostly restricted to batting average, which normally isn't the first indicator of a player aging out. But he is 34 and had only one month (July) with an OPS of .800 or better. I suspect that his issues were mostly mechanical, but it's hard to take a glass-half-full approach with him when he still commands a premium at the position. | |
| 8 | |
| Gelof faked us out once before with a splashy rookie showing in 2023, but his success in 2026 went beyond just the surface level. He added more than 2 mph in average bat speed and shaved more than 10 points off his strikeout rate from the previous two years. Of course, he missed some time with injuries, but if you project his 22 homers and 16 steals over 162 games, they come out to 32 homers and 23 steals. | |
| 9 | |
| If Okamoto simply repeats his 2026 stat line, he'll be well worth drafting here, but that's a big if. The league learned to force-feed him breaking balls, diminishing his power over the course of the year, and his poor batting average and uninspired defense already give him a thin margin for error. His success depends on him piling up counting stats, so any threat to his playing time could be a deal-breaker. | |
| 10 | |
| An early injury to Carlos Correa conferred everyday duty upon Paredes, and it went about as swimmingly as it always does for him, which hopefully means the playing time question won't be raised again. He has little raw power but excels at lofting the ball to the shallowest part of left field, which is generally good for 25-plus home runs, particularly with the Crawford Boxes at his disposal in Houston. His plate discipline elevates him all the more in points leagues. | |
| 11 | |
| Muncy played in a career-high 149 games in 2026 and performed equally against righties and lefties, which may be enough to quiet the talk of decline. Seeing as he's 36, though, it's still going to be on the tip of everyone's tongue, and just because he performed adequately versus lefties doesn't mean the Dodgers were eager to use him against them. The profile is similar to Isaac Paredes, but I think with more playing time risk. | |
| 12 | |
| Improved pull-air and strikeout rates put Mead on the breakout path with a .253/.353/.498 slash line. It also compelled the Red Sox to give up an intriguing young hurler ( Connelly Early ) for him at the trade deadline. They have yet to see any benefit since he got hurt right away. However, Mead is in line to start for them at second base, which would only expand his already favorable eligibility. His swing should theoretically play well at Fenway Park, but he remains largely unproven. | |
| 13 | |
| Like Curtis Mead Schmitt's breakout was interrupted by a midseason injury (torn meniscus), and in some ways, it was the more compelling of the two. He picked up 1 mph in average bat speed and had an xBA (.288) and xSLG (.512) that were 95th percentile or better. He has a tendency to swing at everything, though, which leaves him vulnerable to the right game plan. Also, while Mead's home venue is likely to help, Schmitt's is likely to hurt. | |
| 14 | |
| It's hard to keep giving Bichette the benefit of the doubt when he fails us twice in three years, and by ranking him this low at a weak position, I would say that I'm not. But I'm also not burying him for three reasons: He hit .284 with a .772 OPS over the final four months, was reportedly still feeling the effects of a PCL sprain early in the year, and will only be 29 next year. It's a batting average-dependent profile, and those can be volatile. | |
| 15 | |
| It's even harder to give Riley the benefit of the doubt now that his numbers have declined five straight years, with the biggest drop coming in 2026, but by golly, he still hits the ball hard. The jump in chase rate this year suggests that his issues are more related to mechanics or approach than diminished tools, which leaves the door open for a fix. It's a long shot, of course, but it's glimmer enough for a budget corner infield pick, particularly with his kind of upside. | |
| 16 | |
| Stott ranks 11th for me at second base, which makes a compelling case that it's actually the weaker position, despite third base's reputation. His upside is more limited than the four ahead of him here. Still, I could see him leapfrogging them on Draft Day, depending on how the scarcities shake out (not just positionally but also statistically, with him being a superior base-stealer). | |
| 17 | |
| The jump from seven home runs to 16 made Garcia a premier third baseman in 2025, so when he regressed to only three (albeit in 82 games) the following year, it's probably reason enough to dismiss him as a one-hit wonder. Trouble is that all three came before he suffered a hand injury in mid-May, and I'm not sure he was ever quite right thereafter, needing separate IL stints for the injury. That he stopped stealing bases is another concern, though. | |
| 18 | |
| Arenado seemed to be on his way out as a power hitter, his dwindling exit velocities reaching a tipping point as he failed to deliver 20 homers in consecutive seasons, and this made it all the more shocking to see him bounce back with 30 this year, 16 of which came in the final two months. I'm skeptical of a repeat, both because he's in his mid-30s and because his average exit velocity actually diminished further to the 3rd percentile. If the Diamondbacks are at all to credit for the turnaround, he'll surely enjoy having another season with them. | |
| 19 | |
| Availability can sometimes trump ability, and simply by virtue of starting 151 games for the Twins (and coming off the bench in five others), Lee compiled some pretty good totals in 2026. The only area where you might consider him a plus, though, is home runs, and those came more from an optimal pull-air rate than a natural ability to impact a baseball. Any slippage in health or production would reduce him to mediocrity again.  | |
| 20 | |
| Westburg spent all of 2026 recovering from a UCL tear, submitting to full-blown Tommy John surgery in May, but since he's a hitter and not a pitcher, he should be in pretty good shape come spring training. The 27-year-old was a burgeoning power threat prior to the procedure, showing the capacity for 30-plus homers in a healthy season, and isn't near the batting average liability that, say, Colson Montgomery is. | |

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers vs Brewers NLCS: Series Preview and Injury Report
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE, WI—The Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers are set to renew their postseason rivalry in the National League Championship Series, meeting for the second consecutive year and third time since 2018. While Milwaukee dominated the regular-season series, Los Angeles has owned this matchup in October, sweeping the Brewers in the 2025 NLCS and eliminating them in seven games in 2018.
The Dodgers also swept Milwaukee in the 2020 Wild Card Series, giving them a perfect record in three postseason meetings. Los Angeles has reached the World Series every time it has faced the Brewers in October, winning two of those three trips. Milwaukee will look to change that history after earning home-field advantage with a 103-win regular season.
The clubs met seven times during the 2026 regular season, with the Brewers winning four games and the Dodgers taking three. Despite losing the season series, Los Angeles outscored Milwaukee 27-25, setting the stage for another competitive October matchup.
The first meeting came from May 22nd through May 24th in Milwaukee, where the Dodgers won two of three. After dropping the opener, 5-1, Los Angeles bounced back with an 11-3 victory behind Teoscar Hernández, who hit a three-run homer and drove in six runs. Yoshinobu Yamamoto then delivered seven innings of one-run ball in the series finale, while Andy Pages homered in a 5-1 Dodgers win.
Milwaukee responded when the teams met again at Dodger Stadium from August 13th through August 16th, winning three of four games. The Brewers rallied against Edwin Díaz in the ninth inning to take the opener, wasting a strong start from Roki Sasaki. The Dodgers evened the series the following day behind another quality outing from Yamamoto, with Pages and Tommy Edman homering in a 3-1 victory.
The Brewers took control from there, beating Los Angeles 4-1 behind six strong innings from Jacob Misiorowski before closing out the series with a 6-2 win. Logan Henderson held the Dodgers to one run over seven innings in the finale, while Milwaukee capitalized on defensive mistakes and bullpen struggles to secure the season-series victory.
Despite those results, the Dodgers enter the NLCS with reasons for optimism, particularly after hitting eight home runs against Atlanta in the NLDS. Max Muncy led the way with three, while Freddie Freeman added two as Los Angeles rediscovered its power after a quieter second half. Milwaukee, meanwhile, relies less on the long ball and more on a deep lineup that led the majors with a .258 batting average, .341 on-base percentage and 10.6% walk rate.
The pitching matchup could ultimately decide the series. Los Angeles boasts a formidable rotation led by Tarik Skubal and Yamamoto, both of whom delivered dominant starts against Atlanta. Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow add depth, giving the Dodgers an advantage in established starting pitching. Milwaukee counters with Jacob Misiorowski, who posted a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts during the regular season, but questions remain about his role in the rotation.
The Brewers have the edge in the bullpen, however, after posting the National League’s best relief ERA at 3.40. Closer Trevor Megill converted 30 of 33 save opportunities, while Abner Uribe and Milwaukee’s collection of left-handed relievers give manager Pat Murphy several reliable late-inning options. The Dodgers’ bullpen looked sharper in the NLDS, but sustaining that success against Milwaukee will be essential.
Milwaukee also has defensive and baserunning advantages, ranking among the league’s best in defensive runs saved and stealing 162 bases during the regular season. The Dodgers’ defensive lapses against Atlanta showed how costly mistakes can become in October, making execution especially important against a Brewers team that thrives on putting pressure on its opponents.
Still, Los Angeles has the postseason experience and star power to make another deep run. Dave Roberts continues to prove he can navigate October, and the Dodgers have repeatedly delivered in high-pressure moments against Milwaukee. The Brewers’ 103 wins and regular-season success make them a formidable opponent. Still, the Dodgers’ rotation, power potential, and postseason pedigree give them a path to a third consecutive NLCS victory.
The regular-season results suggest this rematch could be tightly contested. If Los Angeles gets length from its starters, capitalizes on scoring opportunities, and limits defensive mistakes, it has a strong chance to continue its October dominance over Milwaukee. The Brewers, meanwhile, will look to use their bullpen depth, athletic defense, and relentless offense to turn the rivalry in their favor finally.
Pitching Matchup
Game One: Tarik Skubal (LHP) (1-0, 1.50 ERA) vs. Jacob Misiorowski (0-0, 4.50 ERA)
Game Two: Yoshinobu Yamamoto (1-0, 1.29 ERA) vs. TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA)
Game Three: TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA) vs. TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA)
Game Four: TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA) vs. TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA)
*Game Five: TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA) vs. TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA)

*Game Seven: TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA) vs. TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA)
*if necessary
Game Times
Game One: Sunday, October 11th, 5:00 PM PT, American Family Field (FOX, FOX One)
Game Two: Monday, October 12th, 2 PM PT, American Family Field (FOX, FOX One)
Game Three: Wednesday, October 14th, 5 PM PT, UNIQLO Field at Dodger Stadium (FOX, FS1, FOX One)
