item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Boston Red Sox Have Clear Offseason Need
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: The Boston Red Sox offense delivered a disastrous performance in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, getting outscored 18-2 en route to a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees. After an anemic final month of the regular season, one thing is clear: the Red Sox must replace the power they traded away with Rafael Devers in 2025. In the Red Sox's four World Series wins since 2000, they have consistently been among baseball's best offenses. In 2004, they ranked first in runs (949), fifth in home ru
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox offense delivered a disastrous performance in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, getting outscored 18-2 en route to a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees. After an anemic final month of the regular season, one thing is clear: the Red Sox must replace the power they traded away with Rafael Devers in 2025.
In the Red Sox's four World Series wins since 2000, they have consistently been among baseball's best offenses. In 2004, they ranked first in runs (949), fifth in home runs (222), first in OPS (.832), and first in WRC+ plus (114). In 2007, they were fourth in runs (867), 18th in home runs (166), third in OPS (.806), and second in wRC+ (109). The theme continues in 2013, when they led the league in runs (853), were sixth in home runs (178), first in OPS (.795), and first in wRC+ (114). Finally, the 2018 Red Sox were first in runs (876), ninth in home runs (208), first in OPS (.792), and fourth in wRC+ (111).
Of course, for the first three World Series titles, Boston had Hall of Fame designated hitter David Ortiz in the lineup, and the 2018 team posted the best record in franchise history en route to a title. However, this trend isn't isolated to the Red Sox; over the last five years, each World Series-winning team (Dodgers, Rangers, Astros, Braves) ranked top 10 in those four categories.
The idea that power wins you games in the playoffs isn't new, and Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow isn't unaware of it; it was among the first things he said at the 2025 GM Meetings. "I don't want to get so anchored to this idea that the only way to score runs is home runs. We showed that isn't the case. That said, a disproportionate number of runs in the postseason are scored via the home run, and that's not something that we can ignore," said Breslow.
The theory that runs are scored disproportionately via home runs played out in the Wild Card round against the Yankees, who scored nine of their 18 runs on home runs. The Red Sox themselves scored their only two runs of the series via a pair of solo home runs.
Yet, heading into 2026, the Red Sox offense clearly was a bat short, and that proved to be the case throughout the regular season as they finished the year 23rd in runs (689), 26th in home runs (163), 19th in OPS (717), and 17th in wRC+ (99).
A Rafael Devers-sized hole in the lineup
Unfortunately for Breslow and the Red Sox, a massive hole remains in the heart of the lineup where Devers once stood. In his first full season in San Francisco, the former Red Sox slugger hit .258/.340/.525/.865 with a career-high 37 home runs and 98 RBI on one of the worst teams in baseball. Adding Devers' home run total to Boston's would have vaulted them into the top 10 in baseball. Beyond providing a massive power boost to the Boston offense, Devers would also have stabilized the designated hitter spot, where the Red Sox got some of the worst production in baseball.
Devers also has a strong track record of success in the postseason, where he's hit .303/.382/.573/.955 with eight home runs in 26 games, and against the Yankees, against whom he posted .269/.346/.527/.873 in 122 games.
Regardless, Devers was traded, and he is not coming back. However, the team had to replace Devers' impact in the lineup, and ultimately they failed to do that. Willson Contreras had a career year in 2026, but he still profiles much more as a complementary piece to the guy in the lineup rather than being the guy himself.
Plenty of power options were available in free agency ahead of the 2026 season, including Pete Alonso, Kyle Schwarber, and even Alex Bregman. However, ultimately Breslow showed little interest in Schwarber, lost a bidding war to the Baltimore Orioles for Alonso, and was unwilling to include a no-trade clause in contract negotiations to retain Bregman. Instead, pivoting to building the team around strong pitching and defense.
Now that both pitching and defense are in place, Breslow needs to focus on adding power to the lineup because the overwhelming sample size shows that slugging leads to postseason success.

item.title: [MLB.com] Braves-Dodgers NLDS Game 1 FAQ (4 p.m. ET, FOX/FOX One)
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen; Mark Bowman
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- The last time the Braves and Dodgers met in the postseason, a trip to the World Series was on the line. The Braves ousted the Dodgers in the 2021 NL Championship Series, going on to win the fourth championship in franchise history. But since then, Atlanta has not made it past the Division Series round, while L.A. is the defending back-to-back champion. The Dodgers' three-peat bid will begin in earnest when they take on the Braves in the 2026 NL Division Series starting this Saturd
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The last time the Braves and Dodgers met in the postseason, a trip to the World Series was on the line.
The Braves ousted the Dodgers in the 2021 NL Championship Series, going on to win the fourth championship in franchise history. But since then, Atlanta has not made it past the Division Series round, while L.A. is the defending back-to-back champion.
The Dodgers' three-peat bid will begin in earnest when they take on the Braves in the 2026 NL Division Series starting this Saturday afternoon at Dodger Stadium, with triple-digit heat in the forecast.
During the regular season, the Braves outplayed the Dodgers, winning five of their six meetings and outscoring them 26-15. But the postseason is a different beast, and a rested L.A. club will meet an Atlanta team that had to play hard to eliminate Philadelphia from the best-of-three Wild Card Series.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 1 is set for 4 p.m. ET/1 p.m. PT on Saturday at Dodger Stadium. It will be broadcast on FOX, FOX Deportes and FOX ONE.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Braves: TBD
Injuries have depleted Atlanta's rotation. Chris Sale won’t be available before Game 2 on Sunday, and Tyler Mahle won’t be available before Game 3 on Tuesday. As for Martín Pérez, who was placed on the injured list with low back inflammation on Sept. 1, he couldn’t be activated before Game 3. Grant Holmes threw just two innings in Thursday’s win over the Phillies, so he may be asked to pitch the first few innings. Or, the Braves could go with Brent Suter as an opener and have Holmes follow.
Yamamoto had already established himself as a big-game pitcher long before arriving in the Majors, but he took it to another level last postseason when he tossed consecutive complete games in the NLCS and the World Series before closing out the winner-take-all Game 7 on zero days' rest. Yamamoto taking the ball in Game 1 would be the only way to have him available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: Michael Harris II, Matt Olson and Drake Baldwin will have to contend with a lefty in Skubal again after facing two left-handed starters in Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez during the Wild Card Series.
Dodgers: After Shohei Ohtani recovered from right biceps and left knee injuries and returned from the 15-day IL, manager Dave Roberts began using a platoon in the leadoff spot, slotting in Ohtani against right-handers and Mookie Betts against left-handers. The leadoff platoon, as well as other tweaks corresponding to the handedness of the opposing starter, is expected to continue in the postseason.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Braves: Didier Fuentes might be the only reliever who isn’t available. He pitched three consecutive days during the Wild Card Series. Robert Suarez has surrendered an extra-base hit in each of the three appearances he’s had since his right elbow inflammation forced him to the injured list in June. But his velocity was up and he looked more like himself while throwing two-thirds of an inning Thursday. He’ll likely get some high-leverage spots, especially with Dylan Lee struggling most of the second half and into the postseason.
Dodgers: L.A. may not have a set closer this postseason, but Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz all seem to be viable ninth-inning options. Righty reliever Edgardo Henriquez, whose regular season ended early due to a lower back strain, is expected to be activated for the NLDS as long as he comes out of bye week workouts feeling good, bolstering the Dodgers' already solid mix of leverage arms.
Any injuries of note?
Dodgers: Of the players who ended the season on the IL, the Dodgers are most confident about Henriquez returning. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option.
Who is hot and who is not?
Braves: Olson, Albies and Harris all homered in Thursday’s win over the Phillies. Harris went 5-for-11 in the Wild Card Series. Baldwin went 2-for-13 and Acuña was 1-for-9.
Dodgers: In September, Betts (1.112 OPS) and Teoscar Hernández (.965 OPS) were two of the Dodgers' hottest hitters. Tucker (.890 OPS) had his best month by far in his disappointing first season in L.A., perhaps getting hot at the right time.
Freeman dealt with right patellar tendinitis early last month, and he has slugged just .355 since the beginning of July. Ohtani recorded a .666 OPS in his past 29 games, when his biceps and knee injuries flared up and impacted his performance.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Dodgers are bidding for the fifth three-peat in World Series history, and the first since the 1998-2000 Yankees. They would be the first National League team to pull off the feat.
• The Braves and Dodgers will be meeting in the postseason for the sixth time. Atlanta was victorious in the 1996 NLDS and the 2021 NLCS. Los Angeles won the 2013 NLDS, 2018 NLDS and 2020 NLCS.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] What WAR Tells Us about the Dodgers' Postseason Prospects
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers’ roster gives opposing managers plenty to worry about, and WAR helps explain why. It also gives Dodger fans a reason to appreciate players whose contributions can get overshadowed by the biggest names on the marquee. Put hitting, pitching, defense and baserunning on a common scale, and the picture becomes more interesting than a collection of home run totals and earned run averages. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers’ roster gives opposing managers plenty to worry about, and WAR helps explain why. It also gives Dodger fans a reason to appreciate players whose contributions can get overshadowed by the biggest names on the marquee. Put hitting, pitching, defense and baserunning on a common scale, and the picture becomes more interesting than a collection of home run totals and earned run averages.
MLB’s projected playoff rosters rank Milwaukee first (53.7 WAR), Los Angeles second (52.0); Dodgers free-agent acquisitions account for 24.5. That makes for an intriguing October argument: how much should we trust the accumulated value of a roster when the season becomes a succession of short series?
First, it helps to understand what the number actually means.
WAR stands for Wins Above Replacement. It estimates how many additional wins a player contributes compared with a readily available replacement, such as a minor league free agent. A four-WAR player has provided roughly four wins beyond that baseline over his playing time. The comparison uses a standardized replacement level, rather than whoever happens to be sitting on his team’s bench.
For position players, FanGraphs combines batting, baserunning and fielding contributions, expressed in runs. It adjusts for position, league and ballpark, incorporates the replacement-level baseline, and converts those runs into wins. Roughly speaking, about 10 additional runs are worth one win, although the conversion varies with the scoring environment. Position matters because filling a demanding defensive assignment carries value that a batting line alone cannot capture.
Pitchers require a different calculation. FanGraphs starts with Fielding Independent Pitching, emphasizing strikeouts, walks, hit batters and home runs, with an adjustment for infield flies. It accounts for ballpark, innings and the different roles of starters and relievers, then converts performance above replacement into wins. Relievers also receive a leverage adjustment reflecting the situations in which they pitch. Consequently, a pitcher’s ERA and his WAR can tell somewhat different stories.
These are FanGraphs figures, commonly called fWAR. Baseball-Reference uses a different calculation, particularly for pitchers, so its totals can differ. WAR is also an estimate: a few tenths of a win should never end an argument about which player is better.
Here are the Dodgers’ leading contributors on the FanGraphs leaderboard:
| Player | 2026 Dodgers WAR |
|---|---|
| Shohei Ohtani | 6.6 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 4.7 |
| Andy Pages | 4.5 |
| Max Muncy | 4.2 |
| Mookie Betts | 3.7 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2.7 |
| Tanner Scott | 2.4 |
| Tyler Glasnow | 2.4 |
| Tarik Skubal | 2.2 |
| Justin Wrobleski | 1.9 |
| Blake Snell | 1.9 |
FanGraphs figures through the regular season, accessed September 29. Skubal’s entry reflects his Dodgers work.
Ohtani’s total combines 3.7 WAR as a position player with 2.9 on the mound. Yamamoto supplied his value across 185 innings. Pages and Muncy both cleared four wins, an excellent reminder to give them their share of the credit. Scott’s placement alongside Glasnow is striking, too, given how much less opportunity relievers generally have to accumulate value.
For October, the workload details deserve attention: Glasnow accumulated his total in 74 innings, Snell in 42⅔ and Skubal in 62 for Los Angeles. Their season totals describe what they contributed over those opportunities; a postseason rotation presents a different distribution of innings.
That is where I find the strongest argument for the Dodgers. A playoff team can concentrate its innings among its best available pitchers. If those arms are healthy and effective, the version of a club taking the field in October can be considerably more dangerous than its season-long totals suggest. The same principle works in reverse when an important contributor is unavailable.
I would take the Dodgers’ combination of options into any series with confidence. Having several plausible game-changers gives a manager room to respond when an opponent neutralizes one part of the roster. It also gives the lineup a chance to survive a quiet series from a star.
Still, picking Los Angeles over any individual opponent is a different proposition from picking it over the entire field. Every additional round creates another opportunity for a brilliant opposing starter, a costly mistake or a badly timed slump to decide things. WAR can help establish expectations; October still gets to write the results.
For Dodger fans, these numbers support optimism and an appreciation of how many players have helped put the club in this position. The roster has enough talent to make a championship a reasonable expectation. Turning that expectation into another parade remains the most difficult part.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [Chicago Tribune] Column: Can the Chicago White Sox keep succeeding in the postseason without a conventional rotation?
item.dc:creator: Paul Sullivan
item.description: CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff. The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff.
The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. The next-best relievers — preferably one left-hander and one right-hander — are the setup men, the potential bridges from starter to closer.
And the pitcher who is least effective on the staff is the mop-up man, whose main function is keeping the better relievers from being overused.
For years managers used that basic blueprint, or something close to it, to get through the regular season. Then when the playoffs arrived, the best three or four starters went longer because the season was almost over and they could empty their bullets in the biggest games.
But baseball has changed, for better or worse, and now anything goes. Boston Red Sox ace Sonny Gray was removed in the fifth inning of a do-or-die wild-card game Wednesday, and Gray and his teammates grumbled about how the game got to this point.
Which brings us to the 2026 Chicago White Sox, who are trying to win with a “no-rotation” rotation.
Will Venable, the second-year White Sox manager, announced Friday that left-handed reliever Hagen Smith would start Game 1 of the American League Division Series against the Cleveland Guardians, serving as the opener Saturday, as he did in pitching three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild-card win in Houston.
It’s no surprise. The Sox have used openers a league-leading 32 times this season, including Smith’s outing Tuesday. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
But does the no-rotation rotation have its limits, or can Venable’s Sox keep succeeding in the postseason with a bullpen-first strategy?
Venable acknowledged Sean Burke could start Game 2 on Monday, as he did in a four-inning start in Game 2 against the Astros, in which starters Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde both pitched in relief. But other than Burke, it might be a guessing game from here on out.
Can Smith come back to start Game 3 at home Wednesday, giving him three starts in their first five playoff games? Who knows what’s up Venable’s sleeve?
“I think the way it’s set up with these off days, we’re going to leverage the arms that we want to leverage when we want to use them throughout these first couple,” Venable said. “And if that means that one of the guys who we’ve been giving starts to throughout the season takes a bulk role in that, there’s certainly potential for that. But I think you can expect us to mix and match and use our best arms in the most optimal way.”
That suggests Smith and Grant Taylor can be the designated bookends of multiple games, with Jordan Hicks, David Sandlin and Sean Newcomb in the middle and Kay, Fedde and Davis Martin as the wild cards.
It’s almost the polar-opposite approach that then-manager Ozzie Guillén employed in the 2005 postseason, when José Contreras, Mark Buehrle, Freddy Garcia and Jon Garland combined for a 2.84 ERA in 12 starts, leading the Sox on an 11-1 run to their World Series title.
In the five-game win over the Anaheim Angels in the AL Championship Series, the four starters had four straight complete games and combined for 44 1/3 of the 45 total innings, with Neal Cotts contributing the other two outs in the ninth inning of the Game 1 loss. The rest of the bullpen had a nice seat to watch the starters dealing.
“I don’t know if you’ll ever see that again,” Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski said afterward. “Managers just don’t do that anymore. They don’t have confidence to let guys go 120 pitches and throw nine innings.”
In the World Series, advance scout Bryan Little and his crew gave Guillén and pitching coach Don Cooper a near-perfect report on strengths and weaknesses of the Astros hitters. Contreras and Buerhle both went seven innings in the first two wins at Sox Park, and Garland went seven in Game 3 in Houston before the Astros tied it off Dustin Hermanson in the eighth.
Guillén was forced to use his well-rested bullpen when the game went 14 innings but also used Orlando “El Duque” Hernández and Buehrle. After Geoff Blum’s go-ahead home run in the 14th, Buehrle notched the infamous “buzzed save” by getting the final out after having a few beers in the clubhouse. “No more than three … I swear,” he later said.
Buehrle wound up on a Wheaties box, but he didn’t become a legend for his cereal-eating habits.
Game 4 was as old-school as it gets, with Garcia going seven shutout innings, Cliff Politte and Cotts getting the Sox through the eighth and Bobby Jenks closing out a 1-0 win to start the parade plans.
“That type of game is like the ones I watched for 162 games during the regular season,” Guillén said in the celebratory clubhouse.
Venable’s approach in the postseason also mirrors what he has done for much of the season.
General manager Chris Getz knew he didn’t have a dominant rotation in spring training, and opening-day starter Shane Smith was quickly dispatched to Triple-A Charlotte after three starts. Martin, Burke, Kay and Fedde have been the mainstays, though Fedde, who signed at the start of spring training, had only 15 starts in his 33 games.
Taylor has evolved into the de facto closer but can go three innings if needed. He also was used as an opener in April. Seranthony Domínguez led the team 12 saves, even after being dispatched at the trade deadline.
Openers aren’t a new concept. “Bullpenning” has been around for the last decade. Cubs manager Craig Counsell also used openers in last year’s postseason.
But is it possible no team has been as unconventional as the ’26 Sox in this particular run?
“It’s possible,” Getz said during the wild-card celebration. “We weren’t trying to re-create the wheel. We were trying to optimize the group that we had. So much of (baseball) has relied on starting pitching. We would’ve liked to do that. But if we were trying to win games, we had to lean on the strength of the club, and we’ve done that.”
The Sox’s strategy has been criticized, especially when an opener puts the bulk pitcher in a hole. Guillén himself has said on the Chicago Sports Network he’s not a fan of openers.
But if the Sox go all the way without a true rotation, the players may never have to buy a meal or drink in Chicago again. Or at least that’s the adage.
“More often than not I’ll just roll in and buy a drink or buy my dinner,” Blum told me last week in Houston. “But every so often, if there is a hard-core Sox fan in the bar or in the restaurant, there will be a free drink that will show up once in a while.”
So it’s kind of true?
“It still carries a little bit of weight,” Blum said. “We’re not quite the ’85 Bears, but the ’05 Sox do OK.”

item.content:encoded:
Why Royals' Vinnie Pasquantino believes White Sox are 'built' for playoffs appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Vinnie Pasquantino has spent enough time facing the Chicago White Sox to know their bullpen presents a tougher task than the name recognition might suggest. That experience has the Kansas City Royals first baseman believing Chicago can push the Cleveland Guardians to the limit in the ALDS.
The White Sox head into Saturday afternoon's opener after sweeping the Houston Astros in the Wild Card round. Pasquantino sees a pitching staff capable of helping them extend that postseason run.
"In my opinion, the White Sox are built for these series because they can just go to the bullpen," Pasquantino said on The Rich Eisen Show. "If you look at some of the names in the bullpen, as a casual fan or if you don't know the White Sox, you don't think much of it. But having faced these guys, it is uncomfortable at-bats; their pitching coach does a great job…"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"I do think the White Sox are alive in this series for sure."
—@VPasquantino on the White Sox ahead of their series against the Guardians ⚾️
(via @RichEisenShow) pic.twitter.com/RMXt0MCWmC
— SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) October 2, 2026
That assessment carries weight coming from a division opponent. Pasquantino's confidence comes from standing in the batter's box against those pitchers, where unfamiliar names can quickly become difficult matchups.
A reliable bullpen also gives Chicago flexibility in a short series. The White Sox can turn to relief options when a starter struggles or a matchup calls for a change, rather than waiting for an inning to get away from them.
But Pasquantino identified a complication: Cleveland knows those arms, too.
"The disadvantage is that they are playing a team they have played all year. If anyone is going to know the White Sox, it's the Guardians," he said. "I think this series will go five. Whoever plays the little things better will win that series. I do think the White Sox are alive in this series for sure."
The regular-season results support his expectation of a close matchup. Chicago edged Cleveland 7-6, with only a one-run differential between the teams.

item.dc:creator: Pete Caldera; NorthJersey com

PETERSBURG, Fla. – How the Yankees' Bay State duo of Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice performed in the Wild Card Series against the Red Sox – drafted out of Massachusetts – was also a take-a-bow moment for player development. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – How the Yankees' Bay State duo of Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice performed in the Wild Card Series against the Red Sox – drafted out of Massachusetts – was also a take-a-bow moment for player development.
"Just impressive to see these young guys step into the biggest stage at the biggest moment,'' said Yankees captain Aaron Judge, their supreme first-round pick (32nd overall) from the 2013 draft.
Here's a look at the other Yankees drafted and developed players who could impact the best-of-five Division Series against the AL champion Tampa Bay Rays:
George Lombard Jr.
Age: 21
Yankees draft info: 1st round (26th overall) in 2023.
In his first taste of postseason – with 42 games of MLB experience – the shortstop handled his position well and went 4-for-8 at the plate.
"A couple of years ago, he was playing high school baseball,'' Judge said of Lombard, while praising the Yanks' rookie and sophomore class in general.
"Just a really good player,'' Max Fried said of Lombard Jr. "He's got a slow heartbeat.''
Spencer Jones
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 1st round (25th overall) in 2022.
Despite Trent Grisham's return, Jones – who batted .389/1.107 OPS in 59 MLB plate appearances vs. lefties – started in center field against Payton Tolle in the Wild Card opener.
The lefty-hitting Jones was shifted to right field vs. Sonny Gray in Game 2, batting cleanup, with Grisham in center.
Jones went 2-for-8 with a walk and four strikeouts in the ALWC.
Judge's status could impact his late game at-bats, if the captain is on the roster, but the 6-foot-7 slugger has earned his opportunity as a regular in postseason.
Ben Rice
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 12th round in 2021.
Rice destroyed the Red Sox in the Yanks' 9-0, Wild Card Series Game 1 win, with two homers - including a grand slam - among his four hits, with six RBI as the DH.
With 41 homers this year, Rice joined Judge as the only drafted Yankees to reach the 40-homer mark in a single regular season.
Expect Rice to continue batting leadoff against the Rays' right-handed starters. Also, he's a .458 hitter with five homers and a 1.685 OPS in seven career games at the Trop.
Anthony Volpe
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 1st round (30th overall) in 2019.
Volpe started the Wild Card opener vs. the lefty Tolle, going 1-for-3 at second base, a new MLB position for him upon his return; he was optioned to Triple-A with Lombard's early August call-up.
Lefty-hitting Jazz Chisholm Jr., on the bench in WC Game 1, started Game 2 vs. the right-handed Gray and went 2-for-3 with a walk in a clinching 9-2 victory.
Given the Rays' right-handed rotation, Volpe might be a bench player this series, utilized later in games for his infield versatility (including some third base) and as a pinch-runner.
Cam Schlittler
Age: 25
Yankees draft info: 7th round in 2022.
Red Sox Nation has already seen enough postseason Schlittler, helping take Boston out of the last two AL Wild Card Series.
After his 117-pitch scoreless effort in Tuesday's Wild Card opener, Schlittler gets the ball in Monday's ALDS Game 2, on one extra day of rest.
That also puts him in line for a possible Game 5 on normal rest. Both games are at Trop, and Schlittler owns a 1.16 ERA in 17 road starts this year.
Will Warren
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 8th round in 2021.
Moved into a multi-inning relief role in postseason, Warren tossed 1.2 innings (one run) following Fried in Game 2.
He should fit that same role against the Rays, with the ability to take over for a shaky or injured starter, or to provide a bridge to the high-leverage duo of Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick, leading into David Bednar.
Austin Wells
Age: 27
Yankees draft info: 1st round (28th overall) in 2020.
At the plate, the lefty-hitting Wells picked it up considerably after a brutal first four months, but his value behind the plate - and his knack for ABS challenges - has been a constant.
As for defending the speedy, daring Rays, "they love to run and take advantage,'' said Wells, emphasizing the limiting of walks in this series.
Wells has been paired all year with Game 1 starter Gerrit Cole, who praised the "role Austin has played in run prevention'' for a staff that led the league in ERA.
This article originally appeared on NorthJersey.com: How these 7 Yankees homegrown players can impact ALDS vs Rays

item.description: In this week’s wild-card showdown between the Braves and Phillies, where Atlanta prevailed in three games, Chris Sale was a workhorse. In Game 1, Sale posted playoff career highs with 6 ⅓ innings and nine strikeouts. On his throw day, which fell two days later in the deciding Game 3, Sale recorded the last four outs to help the Braves clinch their first playoff series win over the Phillies. It turns out Sale was the one who set the wheels in motion to appear in Game 3. Manager Walt Weiss origina
item.content:encoded:
In this week’s wild-card showdown between the Braves and Phillies, where Atlanta prevailed in three games, Chris Sale was a workhorse.
In Game 1, Sale posted playoff career highs with 6 ⅓ innings and nine strikeouts.
On his throw day, which fell two days later in the deciding Game 3, Sale recorded the last four outs to help the Braves clinch their first playoff series win over the Phillies.
It turns out Sale was the one who set the wheels in motion to appear in Game 3.
Manager Walt Weiss originally had no such plans.
“I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight,” Weiss told reporters. “I didn’t want to put him in that position because I knew that even if he was hanging, he would tell me yes. So, I was not going to bring it up.
“But literally as soon as I stepped into my office this afternoon, he was sitting in the chair across from my desk, and he looked at me, and he said, ‘I feel amazing.’ I said, ‘Well, let’s talk.’
“I told him there was a good chance he was going to get the top of the order at some point in the eighth or ninth. It worked out that way. Was hoping he only had to go one, but he had to get to four outs. But what a warrior, man. This guy — I’ve run out of superlatives for Chris Sale.”
Sale threw 95 pitches on Tuesday and 21 on Thursday, so after the elimination game win, Weiss was unsure about Sale’s status for a potential NLDS Game 2 start against the Dodgers on Sunday.
“It was all about tonight,” Weiss said after the win.

However, Joey Ortiz’s situation is a little more complicated as the team prepares for its postseason opener. Manager Pat Murphy provided updates on both infielders, giving Milwaukee a clearer picture of its available options heading into the series. According to David Gasper of Brewers Daily, Vaughn is a full go this week after overcoming an illnes
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers have received encouraging news about Andrew Vaughn ahead of their National League Division Series against the San Diego Padres. However, Joey Ortiz’s situation is a little more complicated as the team prepares for its postseason opener.
Manager Pat Murphy provided updates on both infielders, giving Milwaukee a clearer picture of its available options heading into the series.
According to David Gasper of Brewers Daily, Vaughn is a full go this week after overcoming an illness that sidelined him. The first baseman is expected to be available as the Brewers prepare for their matchup with San Diego.
That is an encouraging development for Milwaukee, which will want its regular lineup available against a Padres team coming off a Wild Card sweep.
Joey Ortiz Remains Limited Ahead of Brewers’ Postseason Opener
Ortiz’s update was more cautious. Murphy said the infielder’s MRI results were clear, but he will remain a little limited in high-intensity activities ahead of Game 1.
The third baseman has been dealing with a bruised right knee and abdominal swelling. While the imaging results offer some reassurance, his activity restrictions leave questions about how much he can contribute immediately.
Here’s Murphy’s update on Ortiz, shared by Gasper:
Pat Murphy on Joey Ortiz: His MRI results were clear, but he remains a little limited in high-intensity activities as he deals with a bruised right knee and abdominal swelling.
Ortiz’s availability matters because Milwaukee will need to manage its infield carefully if he cannot handle his usual workload. The Brewers will have to monitor his condition as they approach the opening game.
Vaughn’s expected availability gives the team some positive news, but Ortiz’s situation remains worth watching. Milwaukee now has a better idea of what to expect from two important infielders, although the final picture will depend on Ortiz’s progress before the series begins.
The Brewers will hope both players can contribute as they prepare for a challenging postseason matchup.

item.title: [MLB.com] Here's how the pitching might line up for the White Sox-Guardians ALDS
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Scott Merkin
item.description: CLEVELAND -- While battling for the American League Central title last month, the Guardians and White Sox divisional race featured an added reward: a first-round bye in the postseason that would allow the champ to set its preferred pitching plan for the AL Division Series. That’s where we find ourselves now, as Cleveland and Chicago get set for their first-ever playoff matchup. As the AL Central champion Guardians enjoyed a bye this week, they also lined up their staff anchors for the first two
item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- While battling for the American League Central title last month, the Guardians and White Sox divisional race featured an added reward: a first-round bye in the postseason that would allow the champ to set its preferred pitching plan for the AL Division Series.
That’s where we find ourselves now, as Cleveland and Chicago get set for their first-ever playoff matchup.
As the AL Central champion Guardians enjoyed a bye this week, they also lined up their staff anchors for the first two games of ALDS, which is set to kick off with Game 1 on Saturday at Progressive Field. Meanwhile, the White Sox are working through things after they completed a sweep of the Astros in the best-of-three AL Wild Card Series on Wednesday to advance.
Chicago’s plan, understandably, is less settled coming off its Wild Card series, though Cleveland has some uncertainty as well. What could the pitching matchups look like? Let’s take a look.
Guardians
Messick has come a long way in one year. The lefty wasn’t on the Guardians’ roster in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series, following his seven-start debut stint in the Majors down the stretch. This spring, he had to earn a spot on Cleveland’s Opening Day roster. Now, the Guards are hoping he paves the way as they push for October glory.
Messick’s stellar rookie season could make him a finalist for both the AL Cy Young Award and the Rookie of the Year Award. The 25-year-old had a 2.56 ERA (seventh in MLB) in 186 1/3 innings over 32 starts, with 193 strikeouts and 49 walks. In perhaps a good omen, he was particularly effective against Chicago, logging a 2.81 ERA with 29 strikeouts and five walks in 25 2/3 innings over four starts.
If you like pitchers with overpowering stuff, Game 2 could be appointment viewing. This season, Williams racked up 248 strikeouts (second in MLB to Jacob Misiorowski’s 252) in 184 1/3 innings over 32 starts, all of which were career highs. He had double-digit punchouts in 11 of those outings, which led the Majors.
None of those 11 starts were against Chicago, though Williams did record a 3.98 ERA with 28 strikeouts and eight walks in 20 1/3 innings over four starts against the White Sox. His Game 2 assignment is noteworthy because it lines him up to pitch Game 5 (if necessary) back in Cleveland, whereas Messick is lined up for Game 4 in Chicago. Williams had a 2.84 ERA in 18 home starts this season, and a 5.05 ERA in 14 road starts.
The Guardians are still working through their plan here. Manager Stephen Vogt noted Thursday that they want to see how Games 1 and 2 go and what their potential needs are before making a decision.
Why could it be Espino? Of the 14 position players on the White Sox Wild Card Series roster, there were six lefties and one switch-hitter. Starting Espino as an opener for lefty Joey Cantillo could force Chicago to make a lineup decision, such as whether to start lefty smasher Randal Grichuk against Espino, or call his number after Cantillo enters.
Espino served as an opener in Cantillo’s final three appearances of the regular season after the lefty encountered some command issues. Cantillo tossed 15 scoreless innings, allowing five hits and four walks, while striking out 17 batters in those outings. The formula could work in October.
All that being said: The Guardians have a flurry of options, between Espino/Cantillo, Tanner Bibee and Foster Griffin. Stay tuned.
White Sox
Some of the TBDs in terms of White Sox starters were cleared up on Friday by manager Will Venable. It begins with Smith, the rookie southpaw, who gets the same Game 1 honor as he did in the sweep of Houston during the AL Wild Card Series.
“They're a really good team. This will be my third time playing [them] since I got up here,” Smith said Friday. “So just kind of familiar with the guys and their lineup and familiar with the scouting reports against them. We are both good teams. We play hard. They play hard. So it's going to be a good series.“
With Sunday’s off-day, Burke would be pitching on regular rest Monday after striking out eight over four innings against the Astros on Wednesday. Venable confirmed Friday that Burke will pitch on Monday and will not pitch on Saturday, but the skipper did not confirm if it would be as a starter or bulk hurler.
Burke recently joked that the White Sox have 13 pitchers, or 12 in the Wild Card round, but they don’t look at anyone as a starter or reliever. This is not a situation of trying to outsmart the opposition by usage of an opener, but it’s more about Venable and his staff trying to win each game and nothing more. It has produced one of the best Major League Baseball stories this season, so why change now?
Again, Kay would make sense, having last pitched Wednesday. But he might be needed in one of the first two games. Everything is fluid.
One thing to consider: Davis Martin has a 5-3 record with a 3.13 ERA over 15 home starts against a 4-5 record and 4.68 ERA over 14 appearances (13 starts) on the road. Let’s not forget rookie Noah Schultz, who has been impressive working multiple innings out of the bullpen, or rookie David Sandlin, a starter who worked in relief against the Astros. Sean Newcomb has done a little bit of everything this season, with a 3.24 ERA over eight games against the Guardians. So he’s always a possibility.
Don’t overlook Smith coming back, with Venable discussing Smith and Taylor potentially being available for all three games.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Should the Phillies trade Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Why blockbuster deal doesn't make sense
item.dc:creator: Matt Snyder
item.description: The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday. It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so
item.content:encoded:
The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday.
It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so I get it. It happens. We're often prisoners of the moment and emotion is a real thing.
I do want to push back on a specific idea, though, as floated by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic:
Trading Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Don't love the idea, but everything needs to be under consideration. Everything.
Now, be sure that this isn't to attack the writer there, as I have the utmost respect for him and he even said he doesn't love the idea. I can see a lot of people running with this, though, and I'll offer up my opinion that this just isn't a feasible idea for the Phillies.
First off, Harper has a no-trade clause and it's been pretty clear over the last several years that he's now Philly through-and-through and doesn't want to go anywhere. Schwarber also has a no-trade clause with his 10-and-5 rights and now has a family with two young children.
Let's say either or both would accept a trade. Would it help the Phillies other than salary relief?
Schwarber is a 34-year-old designated hitter heading into 2027 with four years and $132 million left on his deal. How many teams would give the Phillies anything of value while also taking on a large portion of the salary? The answer is not that many and it might be zero.
Harper needs to permanently go back to first base and he'll also be 34 years old next season. He has five years and roughly $125 million left on his deal. Again, how many teams would give good value back to the Phillies and salary relief? The number is higher than with Schwarber, but not by much.
This isn't to say neither player is good. Both are very productive offensively. In fact, they were the Phillies' only two good hitters this season. Harper had a 131 OPS+ and Schwarber was at 128 with 100 being the average player at getting on base and hitting for power. No other qualified players on the Phillies were in the vicinity of Harper or Schwarber. Only Bryson Stott at 98 even approached league average. Brandon Marsh finished at 90, Alec Bohm 87 and Trea Turner 81. Yuck.
Schwarber and Harper are much more valuable to the Phillies than they would be to any other team, given the circumstances. And, unless the Phillies are going full-on rebuild, they might as well play out the contracts and try to win with them.
If you look at how things are set up for next season with the pitching staff, a rebuild doesn't make sense.
- Jesús Luzardo made a turn toward ace this season. He's under team control through at least 2031.
- Cristopher Sánchez will likely finish in the top three of Cy Young voting. He's under team control through at least 2032.
- Zack Wheeler showed flashes of being really good while returning from an incredibly tough surgical procedure. He's signed for one more season. He could well return to ace form.
- Aaron Nola doesn't have a tradeable deal, but hey, he had a 10-start stretch with a 2.10 ERA late in the season.
- There were still inconsistencies, but Andrew Painter, at age 23, made big strides during the season and perhaps turned a corner with in Game 2 vs. the Braves. Next year could well be a breakout.
That's a five-man rotation and maybe one of the very best in the majors.
Jhoan Duran is a top-three closer, too.
The starting point here is a great rotation and closer combination, along with Harper and Schwarber being excellent hitters. That's a better nucleus than most teams have. Ownership is committed to doing what it takes to land a winner for the city of Philadelphia and Dave Dombrowski is a front office executive who has proven he's good at making good teams into champions.
Keep taking as many shots at the postseason as possible in hopes that one of these years, the hot streak lines up properly for a championship. We've seen a well-timed hot streak pay off in recent years for teams like the Nationals, Braves and Rangers -- and maybe it'll be the Padres this year? -- so we know it can happen. Hell, the 2022 Phillies were right there.
The team defense needs to improve and there should be some tinkering with the position players, but the foundation here is far too strong to bail on Schwarber and/or Harper, especially when it wouldn't improve the big-league roster in the near-term.

item.title: [Diario AS] Dodgers NLDS roster: Who will make the 26-man playoff roster against the Braves?
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Serrano; Jennifer Bubel
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles. Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeat
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles.
Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeating the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, setting up the Dodgers’ first postseason matchup with the Braves since the 2021 NL Championship Series.
Your 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers. pic.twitter.com/XYs9LzjRIb
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers’ five-day bye gave Dave Roberts and his staff time to prepare their roster, and while most of the pieces are already in place, there are still some important decisions to make before the 26-man NLDS roster is finalized. MLB reports that the final bench spot remains particularly unsettled, while the bullpen could also have an opening depending on the health of Edgardo Henriquez.
Who will make the Dodgers’ pitching staff?
The Dodgers’ biggest strength heading into October is their starting rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow form a formidable group, although Roberts had not formally announced the order entering Friday.
Yamamoto is the leading candidate to start Game 1 against Atlanta. His normal rest schedule is one of the reasons the Japanese right-hander makes the most sense for the opener, as starting Saturday would also give him the chance to be available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
#ITFDB presented by Toyo Tires. pic.twitter.com/TcKpliJrnR
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers also have several pitchers who could be used in relief despite spending much of the regular season as starters. Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan are among the options who could give Roberts additional flexibility out of the bullpen.
Edgardo Henriquez is another name to watch. The right-hander emerged as an important leverage option during the regular season before lower back discomfort ended his year prematurely. The Dodgers planned to have him face hitters during the bye, with an activation for the NLDS possible if he comes through the workout without any problems.
What will the Dodgers’ offense look like?
Shohei Ohtani will once again be the centerpiece of the Dodgers’ offense, but the situation is different from what it appeared to be when the original story was written.
Ohtani returned from the injured list in late September and played in each of the Dodgers’ final five regular-season games. He went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts and one walk during that stretch, but Roberts said the team had no health concerns with its superstar heading into the postseason.
It’s Shotime! On this day in 2024, Shohei Ohtani started the 50/50 club.
This MomenTito’s in Dodger history presented by Tito's Handmade Vodka. pic.twitter.com/cxOEcJyPNK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 19, 2026
Ohtani is expected to remain the designated hitter, with Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base and Max Muncy at third. The Dodgers’ outfield is also largely established, with Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages expected to occupy the three spots.
The lineup could continue to feature some adjustments depending on the opposing starter. Against right-handed pitching, Ohtani has been used at the top of the order, while Betts has taken the leadoff spot against left-handers. That platoon is expected to continue into October.
Who's your Player of the Game? Comment your answer below! pic.twitter.com/tt6sVtGvWT
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 26, 2026
Who gets the final roster spot?
The Dodgers have several candidates competing for what could be their final bench spot: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, and Hyeseong Kim. MLB’s postseason preview identified the decision as one of the biggest remaining questions for the club.
De Paula is intriguing after his impressive first taste of the Majors. The Dodgers’ top prospect hit .323 with seven RBIs and seven runs scored in 11 games before being optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned from the injured list. His performance was strong enough to keep him in the postseason conversation.
But Kim offers something different. His defensive versatility, speed, and ability to contribute off the bench could make him valuable in a playoff series, particularly if Roberts wants another defensive option late in games.
MLB.com Dodgers beat reporter Sonja Chen noted that both De Paula and Kim could have a chance to make the NLDS roster if Los Angeles carries 14 position players and 12 pitchers. The final decision could ultimately come down to whether the Dodgers prefer another impact bat or additional speed and defense.
Rushing and Call remain possibilities as well, meaning the Dodgers have not simply decided between De Paula and Kim.
The other variable is the pitching staff. If Los Angeles carries only 12 pitchers rather than the maximum 13, it would open another position-player spot and potentially allow Roberts to keep more of those candidates.
Dodgers are chasing history
There is plenty more than a division title at stake for Los Angeles. The Dodgers are attempting to become the first team since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 to win three consecutive World Series titles. They have already won three of the past six championships and enter October as the defending champions for the second straight year.
Their first obstacle is now set: the Atlanta Braves. The two teams will meet Saturday in Game 1 of the NLDS at Dodger Stadium, with Yamamoto the likely starter for Los Angeles. Before the first pitch, however, Roberts and the Dodgers still have a handful of decisions to make about exactly which players will be part of their attempt at a historic three-peat.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts. The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? We
item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series
item.dc:creator: Daniel Mader

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff predictions 2026: Expert picks for every ALDS, NLDS series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
October has officially arrived, just in time for the MLB postseason to ramp up.
With all four Wild Card series now over — three of which ended in two-game sweeps — just eight teams remain alive in the pursuit of a World Series title, with the Guardians, Rays, Dodgers and Brewers entering the picture after watching the first round from home.
Some of baseball's biggest stars, from Shohei Ohtani and Jacob Misiorowski to Junior Caminero and Cam Schlittler, will be on full display for the division series. On both sides of the bracket, the question will be whether the teams carrying their Wild Card momentum can now take down a well-rested heavyweight.
With a chance to reset between rounds, the best-of-five ALDS and NLDS matchups begin Saturday. Who will advance to the championship series?
With Wild Card matchups in the rearview mirror, The Sporting News predicts the 2026 MLB division series matchups.
MORE: Complete MLB playoff schedule for 2026 postseason
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 2 Cleveland Guardians
You can certainly debate whether the Guardians (85 regular-season wins) or White Sox (84 regular-season wins) really belong on the postseason stage this season, with neither AL Central squad owning a ton of big-name star power. Regardless, the fact is that Cleveland and Chicago both find themselves with an opportunity to make a serious postseason run in a weaker AL bracket — and the White Sox have already taken advantage.
Chicago enters the ALDS the momentum of its first postseason series win since the 2005 World Series, proving in the Wild Card round that it has the power and pitching depth to challenge opponents. Cleveland, though, has better top-end starting pitching in Parker Messick, Gavin Williams and Tanner Bibee.
These two teams are well familiar with each other; the White Sox won the season series, 7-6. Cleveland's offense isn't very threatening, ranking last among all postseason teams in team OPS (.696) — this matchup will likely come down to how early the White Sox's bats can get to Guardians starters.
Saturday will mark the first time in MLB history that the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland have met in the postseason.
The White Sox began playing baseball in 1894 as the Sioux City Cornhuskers.
The Guardians began playing baseball in 1896 as the Columbus Buckeyes/Senators.
The fact that this is a divisional matchup means it will likely be close, but Chicago's momentum is hard to ignore, and there was only a one-win discrepancy between the sides in the regular season. The White Sox are finally building something serious, seemingly with a new hero every night. The power in Will Venable's lineup is dangerous enough to reach the ALCS.
Prediction: White Sox in 4
No. 4 New York Yankees vs. No. 1 Tampa Bay Rays
It's been clear since the start of the postseason that whichever AL East team emerged from the lower half of the bracket would be favored to reach the World Series. This is the heavyweight matchup of the two ALDS series, featuring elite starting pitching on both sides and some of MLB's premiere sluggers.
Of course, the massive question lingering over this matchup is how much, if at all, Aaron Judge will play for the Yankees. Even as the lower seed, if he's near 100 percent, it's hard not to view New York as the favorite to reach the ALCS; a healthy Judge, alongside Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. and Ben Rice, takes Aaron Boone's lineup to a new level, capable of matching the all-around offensive excellence of Tampa Bay's quartet: Caminero, Yandy Siaz, Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson.
The Rays won this season series 7-6, but it may be the most evenly matched division series. Both sides can roll out a trio talented starters — New York with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole, and Tampa Bay with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and Shane McClanahan — to pair with deep offenses.
Yankees can line up their pitching as follows against the Rays:
Game 1: Gerrit Cole
Game 2: Cam Schlittler
Game 3: Max Fried
Game 4: Gerrit Cole
Game 5: Cam Schlittler
For two reasons, the Yankees are the pick here. For one, between Schlittler and arguably the best bullpen in baseball, New York is loaded with leverage arms. And the Yankees are also riding high off a dominant Wild Card series, biding time for Judge and Giancarlo Stanton to heal. Assuming those two sluggers can at least be used in some key at-bats, the Yankees' lineup is capable of changing games in an instant.
Prediction: Yankees in 5
No. 3 Atlanta Braves vs. No. 2 Los Angeles Dodgers
The Dodgers' path to becoming the first National League team to win three-straight World Series will begin with a matchup against a 94-win Braves squad fresh off a Wild Card win over the Phillies.
Los Angeles' rest advantage could be significant. Even if he's not pitching, Ohtani has been dealing with lingering injury concerns over the last few months. A week off between his last regular season game should only benefit him, not to mention the Dodgers' ability to line up their loaded starting rotation however they choose. With the Braves using Chris Sale in two games against Philadelphia, he may not be available early in the NLDS.
The Dodgers and Braves have built quite the postseason history. 👀🔥
2013 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2018 NLDS — LAD def. ATL
2020 NLCS — LAD def. ATL
2021 NLCS — ATL def. LAD
2026 NLDS — ??? 🤔 pic.twitter.com/mHhbDO9gDX
The top of Atlanta's lineup is potent enough to make this an interesting series, and the team did beat the Dodgers five times in the regular season, but Ronald Acuna Jr., Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies will have to meet the moment in the NLDS. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has pitched well against Atlanta in his career, as have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow.
Even if the Braves' bats can keep things close, it's hard to imagine Atlanta's pitching staff beyond Sale being able to contain Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Kyle Tucker and Mookie Betts over a five-game series. The Braves are a good team, but the Dodgers are far too talented to fall this early in the bracket.
Prediction: Dodgers in 4
No. 4 San Diego Padres vs. No. 1 Milwaukee Brewers
This matchup pins baseball's best team all season, Milwaukee, against one of its hottest over the past month, San Diego. While the Brewers are the clear favorites here, between the best starting pitcher in the game this season and a deep lineup that plays to contact, the Padres do pose some interesting challenges, going 4-2 against Milwaukee in the regular season.
On one hand, San Diego has stars made for October. As shown in the Wild Card round, when the top of the Padres' lineup is on, they're a hard team to beat — Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado, Xander Boegarts, Ty France and Jackson Merrill can look like one of the best 1-through-5 groups in baseball at times. Add in an elite starter (Michael King) and a strong bullpen led by Mason Miller, and there's a path for the Padres to pull off a stunner here.
Most data has shown that the more of a threat a team is to hit the ball out of the yard, the better they'll fare in the postseason. If this is finally going to be the year the Brewers reach a World Series — putting an end to their cycle of regular season success with playoff shortcomings — they'll need to slug more. This is an offense that's outstanding at making contact and getting on base, but has also continually come up short in October and finished second-to-last in team home runs (154) in the 2026 regular season.
Chances are, Milwaukee won't only be able to rely on its strong pitching staff to reach the World Series. The Brewers' bats will need some extra-base hits. But with the Padres' lackluster starting pitching depth, this is still a series the Brewers can claim even if they're not pristine.
San Diego may have some top-end talent and momentum, but the Padres can't match Milwaukee's all-around depth.
Prediction: Brewers in 4

item.content:encoded:
Tonight, the Atlanta Braves hosted the Philadelphia Phillies in a one-off game.
It was a highly anticipated division showdown.
The Phillies chose to put Aaron Nola on the mound… and early in the game, he didn't exactly live up to his managers' expectations.
In the first inning, after four batters, the score was 3-0. Michael Harris II hit a three-run homer after his teammates drew two walks.
Nola ended up pitching for less than two innings, even though his last start (which also went poorly) was five days ago. #RegularSeasonBreak
Ray Kerr, meanwhile, was slated to be an opener for the Braves. But he pitched longer than Nola in his first postseason start, thanks in large part to his defense.
The spin throw from Mauricio Dubón
The pick from Matt Olson
What a beautiful play by the @Braves defense! pic.twitter.com/fpAJ8LPwWx
— MLB (@MLB) October 2, 2026
Kerr didn't allow any runs in 3.1 innings of work. He was excellent.
The Phillies, meanwhile, quickly turned to Zack Wheeler. It was the right move, and manager Don Mattingly will have decisions to make if they advance to the Division Series.
The problem for the Phillies? Early in the game, they didn't put themselves in a position to worry about the series against the Dodgers.
Ozzie Albies went 5-0 with a two-run homer.
The Phillies pulled within 5-1, but the Braves maintained their five-run lead as Matt Olson hit a solo home run.
Then, with the score 6-2 and the Phillies gaining momentum, the Braves brought in Chris Sale. This likely makes up for his bullpen session between starts, but will he be able to pitch on Saturday? Sunday?
Sale hadn't pitched in relief in the playoffs since the 2018 World Series.
So the Braves have eliminated the Phillies. They'll face the Dodgers in the Division Series.
- Russell Martin inducted into the Quebec Sports Hall of Fame.
- Jameson Taillon will undergo elbow surgery, but he hopes to pitch in 2027.
- The playoff schedule.
Created by humans, assisted by AI.

item.title: [North Side Baseball] Don't Stop Him Now: The Breathtaking Brilliance of Pete Crow-Armstrong, One More Time
item.dc:creator: Matthew Trueblood
item.description: Cubs Video It's every human's greatest (if, at times, subconscious or unwanted) wish to be understood—to have others really see us as we see ourselves and grasp what we believe gives life its meaning.
